Madam Speaker, I have two questions for the minister who just spoke. I know he has a very sincere interest in this subject. During the course of his remarks he was speaking very positively, in fact, I would say he was bragging that the government has a number of policies including affirmative action in the public service. He also said at one point referring to descendants of the Chinese Canadian workers on the railway that all Canadians are participating in this countiy of ours.
I would like to ask him how he can justify the lack of action, the lack of results, in the so-called affirmative action in the public service in light of the figures which I have. The percentage of visible minority people in the general workforce is 6.3 per cent; the percentage of visible minority people working in the public service is only 1.58 per cent; and the target of the federal government for visible minorities was half way between, 3.2 per cent.
There is supposedly an affirmative action program to make sure that visible minority people have their fair share of jobs in our own public service. We are failing drastically. I would like him to explain this and to explain what the government is going to do about it, especially in view of the fact that there is a cut-back in public service jobs and it is going to get worse rather than better. If his colleague behind him would stop talking, I would be glad to present the next question.
The next question has to do with a question I raised this morning. How can he justify the goals of multicultur-alism and the goals of this new department which he outlined when the government is cutting back on all funding for citizenship instruction and language training? Does he not think it is absolutely essential to help new immigrants who do not speak English or French and in fact to help many Canadians to become a part of mainstream Canada? That is absolutely essential and it is a federal government responsibility to provide citizenship training and language training so that people can get into Canadian society.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to respond to my colleague who I know has a sincere and deep interest in Canadians of all backgrounds. First of all, I do not want for a moment to say that the world is perfect in Canada. I have not been saying that. That is why we need a multiculturalism department and that is why we need other steps to assist in bringing about a much better world than we have at the moment.
What about the public service?

I was quiet for the hon. member and I hope that she will give me an opportunity to respond as well. What I am saying, first, is that prior to this government taking office there was no affirmative action program for visible minorities in the public service. There is now such a program and obviously it is pointing out exactly what many of us believed but about which we had no true evidence; that being that we were not perfect in the public service as far as its representation and its reflection of Canadian society was concerned. Now we have the mechanism in place to indicate to what extent the public service does reflect Canadian society and now we can move on to the steps to correct that. That is exactly what is happening. I might say that I have been laying a great deal of emphasis on that in my own department and hopefully before too long we will show some results.
Second, in respect of the question of cut-backs in funding, we all deplore cut-backs in funding of everything. I do not think anyone in this House enjoys seeing funding cut-backs not just on these programs but on a whole range of programs as the hon. member knows. If we did not have the fiscal problem that we do now, it
October 3, 1989

would not be necessary. Obviously this has to fit into an over-all global pattern of budget responsibility. I know the hon. member has opposed the goods and services tax and other things of that sort. She does so normally, saying that we can tax not all people but others like corporations. She also says that we can cut out unnecessary expenditures. So far, at least, I have not heard from her or her colleagues about any viable, logical suggestions on how to get the deficit under control. I realize she believes that it has to be under control too. Unfortunately, everything has to be restrained, and this is one of the things, along with housing and everything else, that has to be restrained if we are going to stop spending 35 cents out of every dollar that we take in paying interest on the national debt.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the hon. minister who I thank for defining, at least from my understanding of his speech, that he indeed believes that Canadian contemporary culture is multicultural. I believe he agrees with that. Based on that, I would like to see his reaction to the fact that in Parliament we have Parliamentary standing committees on communications, culture, citizenship and multicultur-alism. I wonder why, if Canadian contemporary culture is indeed multicultural, we have departments of culture and multiculturalism.
Second, another question is in relation to the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, specifically as it relates to human rights. In a speech made to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Rights and the Status of Disabled Persons, the hon. Minister for Multiculturalism stated that in addition to enshrining multiculturalism as a prized characteristic of our national identity, the Act has profound human rights implications. It recognizes the right of all citizens of every racial and cultural background to participate fully in Canadian society bringing to Canada their own style of being a Canadian.
I would like to ask the minister what human rights I, as a Canadian not bom in this country, have as a result of the Multiculturalism Act that I did not have before under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the Human Rights Act and the Citizenship Act.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his questions. As I understood it, there were two questions, the first of which dealt with why there should be a separate Department of Multiculturalism when there is a Department of Culture. Am I misinterpreting the hon. member's question?
There are, as the hon. member knows, all sorts of different departments of government. They serve many, many functions. This particular one I see in the light of the hon. member's second question to me, that being the question of what other rights he has now that he did not have before the Multicultural Act.
I see the whole issue as one of clearing away barriers. Whether it be a special committee to deal with that issue or whether it be a department to deal with that issue, I see the whole concept here as clearing away any and all barriers that there are in the way of Canadians, from whatever background, to the full participation and involvement in the fullness of being a Canadian. If the hon. member does not think there are any barriers, I invite him to look around, but I suspect he does understand that and that is really what this whole thing is all about as I see it.
In my own community, as I said, there are over 60 different cultural groups from all over the world. I think of that community as one where a few years ago there were quite severe concerns from people of other backgrounds about people of yet other backgrounds. Now those concerns have not melted away entirely, but they had been reduced very substantially.
I think that this kind of a mechanism, whether it be the Multicultural Act, the multicultural committee or the multicultural department, is a way of clearing away those barriers, barriers that I know the hon. member realizes exists and would like to see eliminated just as much as I and the government want to see eliminated.

Madam Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak on Bill C-18 to establish a department of multiculturalism and citizenship because I think there are some serious problems with it. It is possible that it could be corrected to be useful, but one of the troublesome things about it is its lack of definition of its job. I notice, for example, in clause 4, page 2, that it says that the minister has the powers, duties, and functions extending to him, including all matters, et cetera, relating to multiculturalism and citizenship and it does not really define it any further at all. It does not say one word about race.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders
I believe that the question of race, race prejudice, racial oppression, racial injustice, is a very serious matter, much overlooked by many of my fellow Canadians and, in fact, one that I did not take as seriously in some past years as I now wish I had because problems that I thought were going away appear to be dreadfully still with us.
Therefore, I think we have to ask ourselves seriously if this bill is for real, is this department proposal for real? Or is it just patronage jobs and top-down propaganda? That is to say, is it really going to focus on opposing, combating and reducing racial discrimination and ethnic discrimination, and if so, how?
One very practical proposal put forward by the New Democrats was that there should be an ombudsman or commissioner, someone who would have statutorily defined duties and powers to whom anyone who felt aggrieved could appeal. Well, that was turned down and it is now sort of mushy, wishy-washy, in a department with a lot of friendly rhetoric but no clear undertaking.
That is not good enough because we have to face the fact that is with us to this very day that Canada as we conventionally call it has racism in its foundation. Canada was self-defined among the French and English arrivals from Europe who chose to kill and dispossess the First Nations of this country and to restrict them to very, very limited ways of earning a living. That is there and that has not changed to this day, not fundamentally.
Now, it is good to be busy about correcting some of the racial wrongs that have been done since then. It is good to correct the matter of the blacks in Canada who have been with us for centuries and are still discriminated against. It is good to correct the matter of the Japanese-Canadians, the matter of the Sikhs, the matter of the Chinese railway workers. When I attended this unveiling of the monument to the Chinese railroad workers that the previous speaker spoke of, I also felt great satisfaction since the idea had been initiated by my motion in Toronto city council in 1979. Certainly more of that is needed and perhaps there should be a monument in Vancouver, if there is not one already.
There is already.

I hear there is already. That is good. But it was appropriate to have it in Toronto where so many of the descendants of the Chinese railway workers are established now.
After founding Canada in part on the dispossession of its First Nations, the aboriginal people have been mistreated from then until now, including through our constitution. Our constitution, when asked to recognize the rights of aboriginal peoples, was persuaded by some of the western provincial premiers to recognize only "existing rights" leaving "existing" of course undefined. What we have learned in the last eight years is that the aboriginal peoples have not been able to make any use of that clause in the constitution. They cannot even get to the bargaining table when their rights are being bargained away.
Nations like the Lubicons have been chiseled out of land rights that were promised to them, the same as the Temagami people in Ontario. There was chiselling and is chiselling on the post-secondary educational rights by a government which has plenty of money for developing certain war projects and therefore has no money for the people of Canada.
There are cramped reserves, poor housing, poor health care services for Canada's First Nations. In the cities, there is much too frequent violence by the police forces and statements, for example, by officials of the Toronto Police Force clearly implying that black people do not have rights and that native people do not have rights.
There is a low intensity warfare being conducted on the homeland of the Innu people. The government is spending hundreds of millions of dollars preparing that; hundreds of thousands of dollars with propaganda to justify it. This is because they are one of Canada's First Nations and they are treated almost as non-persons. This situation cannot be trivialized out of existence by creating a department of multiculturalism or even a Department of Indian and Northern Affairs.
October 3, 1989

I have referred also to the blacks. There is not time to go into all the matters that this department is in danger of overlooking. We have had black people with us for several centuries in some parts of Canada and generally, they were and are poorly treated compared to white people in Canada.
In Toronto last winter and the year before, there were killings of blacks by Toronto police which have yet to be properly examined. It is shocking that when the Attorney General of Ontario dared to permit manslaughter charges to be laid, he was criticized by the president of the police union for having yielded to pressure. No police official of the Ontario government or of metro called that public servant to order for attacking a decision of the attorney general.
Likewise, another police official said, "Well, if people don't like what we are doing, we'll just let the blacks do anything they want and this will become like Detroit". That was a racist lie calculated to create fear in a city which so far has succeeded in avoiding the worst sort of excesses of a city like Detroit.
There is the situation in Nova Scotia and a recent report about Nova Scotia schools with the headline: "There is racism at all levels: Black, natives face barriers in school system, task force finds". That is in a study by Dalhousie University and, of course, there have been many other witnesses to the same point.
In Parliament, there is a book in our parliamentary library called A History of Blacks in Canada by James Walker. Now, to the credit of the Department of the Secretary of State, this was written partly with a grant from the Secretary of State, but only 500 copies were printed. Attempts to find it in bookstores or in Toronto public libraries have failed. Why is it that there was no funding given to the larger distribution of a careful scholarly work on the history of the black people in Canada?
We also know of a recent complaint by Brenda Lem, a Chinese writer, regarding the difficulty of locating works in public libraries by writers of colour. We are not talking about the past, we are talking about the present because the past is too much with us.
As was mentioned earlier by my colleague, government employment does not set the example that it ought to set. To set up a system for reporting and wait five years for a review of the law is a way to avoid doing anything. The government has the means of getting this informa-
Govemment Orders
tion in its own employment or in its Crown corporations without going through such a ponderous process.
We are told by David Vienneau in The Toronto Star that the national labour force participation rate for visible minorities in Canada is 6.3 per cent. The government seems to require only half of that, 3.2 per cent. Even that was failed by the CBC with only 2.1 per cent, Canadian National Railways with 2.7 per cent, Air Canada with 2.9 per cent and Canadian Airlines 3 per cent. It does not matter whether it is public or private employment.
It was veiy interesting that CHUM Radio in Toronto, which employs 1,591 people, had the lowest over-all grade of 1.2 per cent. To be fair, large companies that received higher grades were Canada Post of 11.6 per cent-the first time I have heard something good for a while about Canada Post-the Bank of Nova Scotia with 10.6 per cent and Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. with 5.6 per cent.
That is not a good record for the Government of Canada. Therefore, we have to ask questions as to what this bill is really likely to accomplish. Even the multicul-turalism sector under the Department of State is having questions raised about it. Out of eight senior appointees, that is the deputy minister, the associate deputy minister, the general director and the directors, only one, the appointee on race relations, is a visible minority, Mr. Ajit Mehat. He was made permanent director only last month. For four years that sector had no permanent director on race relations, no established statement of policy or strategy on how it was to work. That does not suggest that during the last four years this matter had high priority under the present government.
The member for York South-Weston has raised a very interesting point as to whether possibly well-meant efforts to help minority groups might in fact, under present circumstances, do them harm, or more harm than good. I think his point is worth examining although I think it requires more careful examination. He mentions, according to The Globe and Mail in Jeff Simpson's article that "the Tories are just catching up to where we were as Liberals".
This invites one to ask where were they as Liberals when they were the government? Where were they on this question of ghettoizing? I was reminded of an article published in Toronto Life in December 1988 by Elaine Dewar, in which she tells us again-we have heard it before, of course, in this House, about something called:

Government Orders
-the Canadian Alliance for Italian Integration and Culture (Alliance for short). It was created in late 1983 and ran until March 1984. It hit the front pages in 1984-just as the Liberal leadership contest got under way. The Alliance had received a grant of $538,000 from the Special Employment Initiatives Program of the Minister of Employment and Immigration to operate a storefront referral service. John Roberts was the minister responsible. Such funds could only be acquired through the recommendation of an MP-in this case, Roland de Corneille. Ian Waddell, NDP MP, had charged the Alliance's real purpose was to put government money into a Liberal riding before an election. Certain persons associated with the party were involved or employed by the Alliance.
She goes on to name names, but I see that my time is running short. However, you can find the names if you want in the December 1988 issue of Toronto Life.
It is possible that the Tories have arrived at where the Liberals were in making a grant like that. It is also possible that they are even falling farther behind in other ways. The Liberals, at that time, were reducing the funding for English as a second language in places like George Brown College where it was taught with professional qualifications, and handing the funding instead to people with no track record in teaching English as a second language, but with reliable Liberal Party connections. But now the Tories are cutting out their program of citizenship instruction and language training, CILT. They have cut it 50 per cent and announced that next year, 1990, it will be cut totally. This particularly hurts immigrant women.
We have had too many years in which ESL and FSL grants were handed out to some immigrants on the grounds that they were destined for the workforce and withheld from others, mostly women, on the grounds that they were not destined for the workforce. Of course, that means that no housewife does any work. There is no work to cleaning the house, making the supper or raising the kids. It also ignored the fact that many of those women did not get even what this department would call work. They worked in factories in cities like Toronto or they worked as domestic cleaners in the houses of more affluent people. But they were denied the opportunity that was given to some to study the English language. Now the CILT program is to be cut out entirely. There still is the employment-related one, but it is not nearly good enough.
What I hope is that if this bill goes to committee, as it should-I understand the government is talking closure. Perhaps it wants to drive the bill through in case it gets looked at too closely. But I hope it will get a very thorough look in committee. I would like it to focus on the existing forms of white racism, racism by people who are white like me against people who are not. That has never been fully acknowledged in Canada and we have corpses to prove it, not only in Toronto, but in many other places, corpses of people of colour, including some of the First Nations, whose treatment cannot be rationally explained except on the basis of systemic, habitual or institutionalized racism. That is not an easy thing to overcome. It would shake the foundations of some of our deepest patterns in some of our institutions.
There is something this government could do in very short order. It would not correct racism per se, although it would ameliorate it a little bit. It would not end all conflict between ethnic groups, but it would do much in a few years to remove the basis of the conflict, and that is to provide instruction in English as a second language, or in French as a second language, to every immigrant old enough to receive such instruction and requiring such instruction.
We have our jokes about our cousins from Glasgow and other parts of Scotland, but until they ask for instruction in English, they probably would be insulted if we gave it to them.
I would hope both of those points will receive heavy consideration if this goes to committee, and I certainly hope it goes to committee.

Madam Speaker, it is interesting that the member started to comment about racism and discrimination in Canada. I would like to commend him. At times, it seems to me, he went a little too far in suggesting that some of the very tragic events in Toronto were race related, even though a number of people have gone so far as to suggest that.
I do not think one has to go to that extent with respect to the killings in Toronto of blacks by police officers. One only has to look here in the House of Commons, across the way, if one wants to cite examples of racism and discrimination. There are members from the Conservative side of the House who are actively seeking and circulating petitions asking the Government of Canada not to allow Canadians of Sikh origin to be members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That is the net effect of their objection. They are saying that it is improper and unacceptable for Canadians of Sikh origin
October 3, 1989

to wear their turbans while members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. There are people here in the House of Commons exhibiting an abysmal ignorance and an abysmal and shocking degree of discrimination when it comes to talking about participating.
I would like the member to comment. Just a few moments ago, the minister of housing, who spoke one tune when he was on this side of the House-that is as a person outside of cabinet-and is speaking another tune when he is in cabinet, went on for a period of time, to the applause of some of his colleagues on that side of the House, about the first government to do this and the first government to do that. But he did not comment about his colleagues circulating the petitions. He did not comment about what is the actual track record of this government. I would like the member from Trinity- Spadina to expand a bit on the track record of the government.
It is fine to talk about affirmative action and about pay equity, employment equity legislation. It is fine to talk in words, but one has to examine the actions. The bottom line was confirmed by the Secretary of State for multicul-turalism just a few weeks ago when he was speaking to Conservatives gathered here in Ottawa at a national convention of their party. He said something to the effect that Conservatives view ethnic communities with distrust and disdain. Perhaps it was the other way around, perhaps it was the ethnic communities that were viewing the Conservative party with distrust and disdain.
But the fact remains that when it comes to general elections the overwhelming majority of Canadians of origins other than French or English vote for the Liberal party. That is because the Liberal party has been leading on the issue of equality. It was the Liberal party that gave Canada the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms that enshrines in our Constitution the equality of each and every Canadian.
You have indicated that my time for commenting is expiring, Madam Speaker. I would like the member for Trinity-Spadina to comment further on the track record of the Conservative government when it comes to equality among all Canadians.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for leaving me a few seconds. I want to comment on what I think is a more serious matter in relation to the Sikhs, and that is the action of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in writing to the then Minister of Employment and Immigration to urge him, apparently successfully, to change the established procedure for determining the status of a refugee claimant. A Sikh from India who had claimed refugee status here had been recommended after due process by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, then the responsible body, to the Minister of Employment and Immigration as a refugee.
After the Secretary of State intervened, the minister appointed another committee of people who were not contaminated by any direct knowledge of refugee affairs. They were from the department of immigration but they did not know anything about refugees professionally, and they reversed the decision. The first committee of appropriate people had unanimously found this person to be a refugee. The second committee obediently and unanimously found this person not to be a refugee.
At the same time the Secretary of State was found to be complaining because already two or three out of several thousand Sikh refugee applicants had been found to be refugees. Apparently, from what he said in his letter, as published, this was thought perhaps likely to hinder commercial or other relationships with the Government of India. I think that was a much worse signal than anything else I know of that this government has done on the matter of bias against the Sikh people.
There are other examples. There was the letter urging other government people not to meet with certain groups and so on. But to endanger a man's life by such a dubious process, legally a very, very doubtful process if not plainly illegal, on the basis and in the context of such racism was a very bad example for the minister to set.
On the matter of the turbans, I have not seen the petitions. I have read about discussion of the matter in the newspapers and I think it must surely be capable of being resolved reasonably between the Sikh community and the RCMP, and I hope they will be allowed to resolve it.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, the member for Trinity-Spadina also mentioned in passing the letter written by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would like him to comment a little further about a letter that was sent to provincial premiers urging premiers and politicians at other levels of government to boycott, not to attend, events put on by certain groups in Canada.
When questioned about that particular letter here in the House of Commons, the minister did not have a justifiable or reasonable explanation as to why as a minister of the Crown, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he would be asking colleagues in this House to boycott legitimate groups in Canada, namely several Sikh organizations in Canada which have done nothing wrong and are legal and legitimate. Why would he ask people to boycott them? Would he suggest, or would the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina comment on whether he believes that that might be a further example of a level of discrimination on the other side of the aisle.

Madam Speaker, I am glad the hon. member heard some of what I was saying. I will repeat the rest of what I said on that. Yes, it is an example of discrimination, as I said a few minutes ago, from the other side of the aisle, as he calls it.
I could enlarge on it a little bit. I received a letter from the hon. minister cautioning me after I had met with a certain group. Now it did not forbid or anything like that, but it said "please get in touch with us before you go to speak with such a group". I regret that the matter was treated as though it were confidential. I do not particularly relish the idea of being given reasons why I should not meet with a group and then being told not to tell anybody. I wish he had put the reasons in his letter. I have since met with other Sikh groups and will continue to do so, but I really think the minister ought to clear up his position on that point if the government is going to have a credible Department of Multiculturalism.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate, the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the multiculturalism debate today. I have just listened to many very interesting statements and speeches on the topic and subject now under consideration. Personally, I prefer to begin in French and continue in English and maybe later, I might say a few words in Italian, because I consider myself, like some of my colleagues, a symbol of this
multiculturalism that we are talking about today in philosophical and practical terms.

It gives me great pleasure to be able to address the essence and soul of Canada with this Bill C-18, an act to establish the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship, even though the designation should be vice versa. To date from this government we have been given merely a callous display of the government's economic philosophy, that is up to today. It is an elementary market economics where laissez-faire prevails, but then only in circumstances decreed by the Conservative agenda as befitting of a continental sweep under which all matters economic must, by force of magnetic or deliberate policies, push and pull Canadian citizens into the orbit of a state whose greatest claim to historical fame is the amassing of unprecedented military and economic power at the expense of numerous nations, peoples and values.
These values need to be re-examined periodically if we Canadians are to keep our sights on a vision that will set us apart from our sister nations as a people whose definition of the human condition is a cut above the others.
It would appear that we lack neither the qualities nor the ingredients for we are at the very least capable of saying the right things. As an example, we pride ourselves on our multiculturalism policy. We have heard much of that today. In fact, today we propose to establish a department to deal exclusively and singularly with all matters multicultural.
Before asserting that we are on the road to salvation or on a road to perdition on the matter, I think it behoves us to cast a momentary, though not casual, glance at what multiculturalism means. I caution, not what the nay sayers in our midst would have it mean, that the aim that the word was intended to stimulate as a goal for which all citizens capable of its achievement could rightly be conferred the adjective "great".
Multiculturalism, so simple a word, so profound its concepts. Cultures, different, unique, each in its own way, none superior or inferior to the other, existing in harmonious, productive interaction; each confident and secure in its values-defined and reshaped in continuous manner, in contact and interplay with others, in a changing environment which hones values tried and true and nurtures on tested, applicable new ones.
October 3, 1989

The main tenets, the main principles embodied in multiculturalism are familiar to all whose historical perspectives go beyond the mere parochialism of personal experience. For that in a global, international context is surely as inhibiting and as restricting as it is limiting.
Let me make clear that when we speak of multiculturalism we are not breaking new ground, by no means, by no stretch of the imagination. The concept of equality among all men, all women, universal brotherhood, the rule of law in western civilization is not new to Canada. They date at least as far back in history as Alexander the Great in the 4th century BC, pre-Diaspora Israel, and in more recent times to the emperor Caracalla in the 3rd century AD when with a single stroke he bestowed citizenship upon the several and disparate parts of the Roman Empire, thus giving equality before the law, equality of access to decision making without-and this is important-a priori transformation into something else.
Thus we could see in an historical perspective that one could acquire Romanitas without being a Roman. One can become Canadian without having been born here. An individual in the past, as today, could retain his traditions, do business, participate in the local or larger economy, enjoy the privileges of citizenship, fulfil the obligations incumbent upon a holder, and yet not give up his or her identity religious, cultural, linguistic. He or she needed only obey the laws which he or she could shape.
I could easily in that description have referred to our own country Canada-citizenship, the rule of law, tolerance, brotherhood, multiculturalism. It seemed then as now a logical solution to problems emerging when different races with unique religious backgrounds and the modi vivendi that emanate from them, with different needs, aspirations, with peculiar social units and economic organizations for their realization, were brought about and brought together. A lingua franca, though not indispensable, facilitated the functioning of the marketplace and the exchange of both ideas and culture.
Government Orders
Multiculturalism, by its definition, encourages and stimulates that exchange in a non-threatening environment. It does not confuse culture with language, but it recognizes that language both as an extension and as an expression of culture is the vehicle for finding common values that transcend different cultures. Language bridges and opens doors to peoples, to markets, to ideas. It does not set apart nor does it exclude or seclude.
Canadians face the unhappy condition of being governed by a party that has blurred the distinction between culture and language and in fact has come to equate the one with the other, all to great detriment. It has downgraded the word "culture" to a national or racial designation and has caused Canadians to seek security of being in the refuge of assimilating, voluntarily or otherwise, in the so-called cultures of the two main language groups, an exercise, as some of my colleagues to my left have noted, that has had the effect of marginalizing Canada's visible minorities in particular. This ethnocul-turalism is not multiculturalism.
Any noble Canadian worthy of the adjective should react vigorously against the deliberate refutation of the realities of a new and expanding Canada. To say one believes in multiculturalism is merely to accept what is; a thriving expression of the ultimate definition of individuality grouped in as small or as large units as per individual preference, living according to values commonly accepted by those units and sanctioned by the acquiescence of a duly constituted larger jurisdiction.
As an example, Europe, whose countries and peoples have histories dating back as far 1000 BC, is now realizing that one builds on common ideas, on common needs, on common experiences and that differences are valuable and can be reciprocally profitable conditions that should be nurtured rather than legislated away.
Where are we going by way of contrast? Legislative, attitudinal or systemic discrimination are too ephemeral in their results, too energy consuming in their efforts, to interest our talents, and we squander opportunity.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders
Yet, as a country we have the tools to be proactive, and aggressively so, if only we through our government would seek out those with open minds to be the custodians of our emerging culture, to be the proponents of a sociocultural philosophy that would make us the lighthouse of social organization in this world.
Look for a moment at the ministry of culture and its dependent Crown corporations, councils, agencies through which we nurture those English and French elements that some would have us believe are mainstream culture. I notice that my colleague from Scarborough Centre, who is at one with me on these issues, is dutifully paying attention and I thank her for so doing.
Look at the ministry of communications and the implements through which it disseminates bilingual Ca-nadianism. Again, mainstream and exclusive.
What a puny little brother beside these Anglo-Franco giants is this little sop to speak for Canada's official multicultural policy. What a testament to this Tory party's rejection of the validity of multiculturalism as anything more than a trite, token recognition of the existence of an inferior folk who comprise that one-third of Canada's population, the only growing portion of the population whose contribution and role in nation building will persevere in spite of the regressive small minds who refuse to accept the inexorable tide of progress.
I am pained to admit that for the disdain with which the government accords this pitiful and reluctant gesture the new Canada will wrest from its hands those tools of nation building which its small mindedness clutches so jealously. Would that the minister who proposes this legislation could have been more forceful in his cabinet we would have need of such advocacy. He might have convinced his government that the occasion for progress was not of the passing.
The ethnocultural communities do not need a special department to represent them, even if the principle of multiculturalism still does. But those communities will accept this condescending administrative token to their cultural uniqueness and recall with methodical anger the manner in which the minister has thus trivialized that uniqueness as his government goes about destroying our country through language debates and constitutional reform that is expected to enshrine established position.
That's absolute nonsense.

I know the member opposite will probably be interested in the rest of the speech because it will be a lesson for him to take to his committee as chairman of multiculturalism or as the new cultural car.
How illusory, how unfortunate, how tragic, how foolish to engage in cheap partisan gamemanship without making even the slightest effort to acknowledge that multiculturalism is first and foremost-are you listening-about culture, about Canada, about how Canadians see themselves, how they define their values, how they shape their identity.
To relegate these values and identity to folklorish song and dance is to deny history and to insult the great traditions and heritages; legal, literary, philosophic and artistic contributions of a substantial portion of our population to the history of mankind.
Once culture was thought to indicate a level of learning and sophistication not commonly evidenced; in short the ability to see beyond the meagre horizons of mundane needs, the ability to approach godliness by creating or refining an expression of the human condition, a condition that transcends the individual histories of people everywhere.
Respect for those histories is being subordinated to the pressures that an insecure people impose on others to assimilate, to efface one's identity in return for yet another's as a sign, perhaps, of homage or fealty to some vague, self-proclaimed superior culture in the name of national identity.
Insecurity is a shaky foundation for any identity. One does not acquire Canadianism by becoming anglophone or francophone, by changing one's name, or by denying one's heritage. An early 20th century playwright philosopher, Luigi Pirandello, said it best in Italian when he said: "Cost e se vi pare", and in English: "You are what others see you to be".
I am proud to be identified for what I am-Italian Canadian, for I am the sum total expression of the experiences of my parents and all of my ancestors, experiences of 3,000 years of historical achievement through which they have learned from and internalized the experiences of great civilizations of this globe-the Oriental, Indian, Hellenic, Hebrew, Egyptian, Arabian and others. Look at the talents and energies that people from these areas bring to our country. Should they apologize for the fact that their historical perspective is measured in millennia rather than in decades?
October 3, 1989

The focus of our multicultural policy should be to integrate these prodigious experiences and talents into our mainstream. They are in fact our culture. We can do that only if we acknowledge their merit and allow individuals with proven merit from their midst to take leadership roles.
The economy and the arts have witnessed their immense productivity and impact. Politics, bureaucracy and the national media will surely follow-fifth columnists notwithstanding.
Our government should be setting an agenda wherein multiculturalism as the operative ethos permeates all levels of government but at the very, very least the ministries of culture and communication. It is an ethos that would both integrate newer Canadians, showcase their heritages and provide expression for their talents and merits.
We are offered a distant second best with this department, but Canadians of origins other than English or French are accustomed to building on scraps.
[Editor's Note: Member speaks in Italian.]
As the government continues to bog itself in the centuries old language wars the rest of us will continue to construct a Canada in which all Canadians will share proprietorship equally, equality based on the acceptance and promotion of a multicultural ethic.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the member who just spoke to clarify the confusion that certainly is in my mind, and I imagine it is in the minds of other people, about the Liberal position on this Multiculturalism Act.
Earlier today we had I think three Liberal members from the Toronto region who seemed to be opposed to the idea of a multicultural department. In fact if you carry their thinking a little bit further it seemed that they were opposed to multiculturalism, period. In one case they saw this as something that would perhaps reflect heritage issues. A couple of them said that they felt this would ghettoize Canadians who were not from either French or English speaking origins. One member in particular felt that we should not have a separate
Government Orders
ministry of multiculturalism but that this should all be under the Department of Communications. He also seemed to suggest that racism and job discrimination against visible minorities would just disappear by some magic. In my party's opinion, this is one of the main needs and should be one of the priorities of a multicultural department.
I would like to ask him whether he agrees with their opinion. I gather from what he said that he does not. He was complaining that the multicultural department was not strong enough, that it was really just token recognition of a third of Canada's population, I think he said. I am confused and I am sure the public is from the point of view of what is the Liberal position. Does he agree with the speakers who spoke earlier?

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the questions. They were very craftily put with very wise insight into the questions themselves.
I am not sure that we need to trivialize the discussion further by highlighting the fact that there are various opinions on the various aspects and components of multiculturalism and about this bill, because this bill has given rise to an opportunity to debate the issues, to debate all components and aspects of multiculturalism. You quite rightly alluded and pointed to the fact that many of us, unfortunately, have begun to equate multiculturalism with racism or with multiracism. It goes much beyond that.
It is a fact of life that there are many who have a different origin than another and have a different colour than another. None of that should stand in the way of progress and in the way that we deal with each other. None of that should stand in the way of people developing policies and having access to government, access to bureaucracy, having delivery of services, having delivery of a vision of Canada that applies to each and every one of them individually and collectively in the way equally that it applies to all others.
And so when you ask me what is the position of the Liberal Party, it has been one that has been open to the infusion of new ideas. It has been one that has been open to the infusion of criticism.

October 3, 1989
My own personal view, and I gave it to you, was that this particular bill does not go nearly far enough. I made some suggestions, and I thank you for having listened to it as well, that the minister should take our directions into his cabinet and indicate strongly to all cabinet members that this is not simply an issue of multicultur-alism, an esoteric definition that we file away in a library, but that it is in fact an explanation and an indication of the directions that should guide all of our policy makers, be those policies in the economic domain, be they in the cultural domain, or in a social domain.
The most important part is to recognize just what are the needs of Canada, what are the needs of all Canadians. This party has continually worked on making sure that the definition and the system by which we arrive at such conclusions have always received the analysis and the scrutiny that they merit. We are not dealing with trivial matters.
We are dealing with the soul and the essence of this nation. For those of us who are looking for the definition of Canada, we offered it up today. I was glad to be a part of that debate because it gave me an opportunity to shape that definition if even ever so slightly. I thank the member for drawing the public's attention to the fact that the Liberal party has always been in the vanguard of honing that type of definition, of developing that kind of contact and of developing as well the resources and the abilities of politicians and the political system to address the needs that are what they ought to be, and that is to make government function for all those who sustain it, for all those who co-operate in developing that process which creates a government and a political body.
To the hon. member who has attempted to focus a direction and a purpose to where all of these debates would lead, I know that her party favours the kinds of decisions that we have acclaimed today. I know that her party along with members opposite would love the opportunity to continue to debate exactly where we should be going because there are many, many vacuums that have to be filled in this particular bill. While we accept it as a sop-and I said that deliberately-it is but that we must go from there to build and to build even further in order to provide for Canada that basis, the foundation from which we can go into the next century.

speechtext: It being 2 p.m. the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from Cambodia, a nation plunged again into civil war, a nation just beginning to recover from the 1975-79 slaughter of an estimated two million men, women and children under the barbaric Pol Pot Khmer Rouge Party.
This time, the blood of thousands of Cambodians will be on the hands of China and the west, including Canada. Canada continues to support the Khmer Rouge at the United Nations, has remained silent as China has resupplied and rearmed the Khmer Rouge, supported the return of the Khmer Rouge to power sharing in Cambodia, and gave $1 million in aid to resistance forces in Thailand after various NGOs and United Nations officials admitted the United Nations has oversupplied these camps which, in turn, supply the Khmer Rouge soldiers and the black market.
While I appreciate that the Secretary of State attended and participated in the Paris Peace Conference, Canada's policy toward Cambodia is at least morally wrong and probably politically wrong as well.

Mr. Speaker, it is my distinct honour and privilege to rise this afternoon to pay tribute to the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires.
These dedicated men and women have served in a branch of Her Majesty's active regular forces, the Canadian forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or were members of allied nations who served with Canadians in time of war.
October 3, 1989

I can attest to their outstanding service to the country, in the provision of dignified and purposeful employment for those who have already served their country and wish to continue to do so. Their pride and camaraderie sets an excellent example and the value of this quality to the rest of our country and their respectful rapport with the public has become a time-honoured institution in Canada.
I know I speak for the right hon. Leader of the Opposition and, indeed, for all my colleagues in paying tribute to the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires on their fiftieth anniversary.

Mr. Speaker, this week, October 2-8, 1989, marks the fifth National Family Week to be celebrated across Canada.
National Family Week gives every Canadian an opportunity to acknowledge the efforts of all family members who show concern and care for each other.
Few among us would deny the importance of the family as a social unit. Although the role of the family has evolved along with contemporary society, it remains the most basic social structure of our time.
In four short years National Family Week has grown from an imaginative idea to a full-fledged nation-wide celebration. Take advantage of the opportunity for the growth and discovery that National Family Week represents.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans referred to the appointment of Don Tansley as a replacement member on the free trade panel studying landing regulations for B.C. salmon and herring.
The Canadian chair of the panel has the right to decide whether or not to reconvene the panel and hear evidence. Can we assume from the parliamentary secretary's comments that further hearings will be held?
There are thousands of British Columbians, 70 per cent of whom are women, many of these of visible minorities, who will lose their jobs if the final decision goes against Canada. As well, Canada will lose its sovereign right to control its own resource.
It is essential that this government stress in all future hearings the importance of controlling our resource. We must maintain B.C.'s well-earned reputation for the quality of our salmon and herring products.
We must protect our investment in the most modem and efficient processing facilities in the world. We must do all within our power to protect the jobs of thousands of British Columbians working in our fish processing industry.

Mr. Speaker, for months, those involved in the economy of Abitibi-Temiscamin-gue have been trying through CRDAT to meet with Air Canada executives on the future of this carrier in the region.
Without consulting the people of our great region, the President of Air Canada and his gang of high-flyers in their ivory tower in downtown Montreal decided yesterday to send letters and press releases announcing that Air Canada would stop serving Val-d'Or and Rouyn-No-randa, Quebec as of February 4, 1990.
As a remote region, we are entitled to receive the best possible service; for us in northern Quebec, the DC-9s are what highways and subways are to the South.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to see these employees whom I have known for 20 years leave with their families and children and I urge Mr. Jeanniot to reconsider his position and come and see us in the Abitibi.

Mr. Speaker, as a result of Bill C-21, the government's bill to cut unemployment insurance benefits, Newfoundland will lose $82.7 million; Prince Edward Island will lose $15.5 million; Nova Scotia will lose $42.1 million; and New Brunswick will lose $64.8 million.
The Government says that this money, money that was set aside to help the unemployed buy their groceries and pay their rent, will be redirected to development and training. But there is no legislative provision in the bill that this money will go back to those provinces from which it is taken.
Why does the government not amend this bill to ensure that the $800 million taken from the unemployment insurance fund for development will go proportionately to those provinces where there is the highest unemployment in this country?

Mr. Speaker, the people in Elk Island recognize that Canada's deficit and national debt are serious problems. We all know that fighting the deficit is not an easy job. We know that we cannot leave this burden for our children to deal with in the future. We must do something now.
Over the past several weeks much has been said in Elk Island about taxation. People have told me that we are taxed too much. If we must change the federal sales tax to fight this monstrous deficit, if we must accept the GST, then let us make sure we cut spending too.
The Canadian Government must make some tough management decisions-cut out the waste, cut out the inefficiencies, reduce spending, and improve the tax system.
Let us work together to reduce the deficit. Let us all work together in this country to build a stronger economy. Let us work together to build a better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to a tremendous political development taking place in my province of Alberta. After more than 100 years without any action on meaningful Senate reform, the government and people of Alberta are taking action.
On October 16, Albertans will go to the polls to elect the nominee for the Senate vacancy. Six outstanding Albertans are contesting the position, including my party's candidate, Reformer Stan Waters.
A handful of Tory MPs and cabinet ministers have seen fit to fight against this process and the entire spirit of true Senate reform. But I am confident that the Prime Minister will join the political pioneers of Alberta and endorse this action by appointing, without delay, the first Senator ever to sit with the consent of the people.

Mr. Speaker, for all the fine words we have been hearing from the Prime Minister concerning how much he and his government are doing for Atlantic Canada, the truth is that the government's policies are short-changing the region and reinforcing regional disparities.

According to a study conducted by the Economic Council of the Atlantic Provinces, federal government funds for industrial assistance have declined steadily since the Conservatives took power in 1984. Furthermore, in 1987, the amount of these subsidies fell below the national average.
In 1980, Atlantic Canada received $2 billion in federal aid compared to $4.4 billion for the rest of the country. In 1987, they received only $631 million while the rest of the country received $8.2 billion in federal aid.

Is this what the Prime Minister means by regional development, Mr. Speaker? How can the Prime Minister reconcile this sad truth with his repeated statements that the Atlantic provinces have never had it so good?

Well, Mr. Speaker, under this government Atlantic Canadians have never had it so bad, and they have never been short-changed so much. Numbers don't lie.

Mr. Speaker, I pay tribute today to the Republic of South Korea as it celebrates its national foundation day.
It was not long ago that Korea and its impressive capital of Seoul were the very picture of devastation as a result of conflict which tore apart a people and culture as ancient as history itself. The Republic of South Korea has now developed a political and economic growth which is making it the envy of the world.
The Canada-Korea Parliamentary Friendship Group believes that closer co-operation with South Korea as a valued partner in our Asia-Pacific diplomacy is a worthwhile result. As chairman of the group I speak for all members in extending congratulations and best wishes to the national assembly and people of South Korea, and our thanks to Ambassador Park and his excellent staff at the embassy for all of their support and co-operation, with sincere wishes that our countries continue to enjoy good relations in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I rose in the House to acknowledge Family Week and to note that 1.2 million children in Canada live in poverty.
Today I rise to draw the attention of the House to the results of an inquiry into hunger in Regina released yesterday by Mayor Doug Archer. This report noted that in a community with a population of 180,000, 5,500 meals and 6,000 boxes of food a month are distributed by community groups.
It is easy to write off numbers. It is easy to blame the poor for their plight. But the reason they are poor is that they do not have work or money to buy food. Surely, no one here honestly believes that a family would go hungry if it could afford to buy food.
The House must be shocked to learn that 34,000 people in Regina live below the poverty line and are hungry-34,000 people in the heart of the province that is the bread-basket of the world.

Mr. Speaker, the Times Review, a newspaper in my town of Fort Erie, headlined a story this way, "Fort Erie booming", and continued, "This community is building its way to record heights." Building permits to the end of August totalled a record setting $32,359,000. This tops the town's 1988 figures of $26.4 million for 12 months.
The Niagara corridor is strategically positioned to benefit from the free trade agreement. Half the population of North America is within a one day's drive of the Niagara peninsula. This represents tremendous opportunities. The free trade agreement has helped to stimulate the great growth that we are enjoying.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State responsible for Multiculturalism made what Canadian Macedonians believe to be offensive remarks.
This summer the minister attended a conference in Greece hosted by the Pan Macedonian Organization where he said, among other things, that there is no Macedonian nation.
Does the minister not realize that to deny the distinctiveness of the Macedonian community in Canada is a serious affront to this group? Will the minister apologize for this statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I want to pay tribute to the men and women who continue to serve this country so well in uniform, members of the Canadian Corps of Commissionaires. We, who work in Ottawa are particularly aware of the courteous, efficient presence of the corps. Our government buildings are kept secure by those smartly dressed uniformed men and women.

Oral Questions
Hon. members probably know that the corps members must be former members of the Canadian Armed Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police or our allied forces.
Today, the Corps of Commissionaires has over 11,000 members in 18 divisions across Canada.
This year marks the fiftieth anniversary of the Ottawa division started in 1939 with just four members. It now has a strength of 2,200, and is the fourth largest non-government employer in Ottawa.
I know the House will join me in congratulating the Ottawa division on 50 years of super service and in sending our best wishes to all commissionaires across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this House held a long and serious emergency debate on Canada's state of preparedness to deal with marine spills and particularly those of crude oil. This resulted from the tragic Nestucca and Exxon Valdez spills and the continued deterioration of our marine environment from chronic unreported spills.
Rather than hold a full public inquiry, the Prime Minister chose to spend millions of dollars on a review. The interim report was released yesterday. It is pathetic. Its 17 short pages reveal just how superficial the mandate and terms of reference really are.
The recommendations reveal a process that will neither seek nor find the kind of solutions required to protect our marine ecosystems. The report operates from the premise that existing technology, ships and barges will simply carry on.
On page 3, the panel states that they are comfortable with their mandate which excludes offshore exploration and development, excludes alternative modes of transporting oil and other chemicals and excludes energy conservation.
The review is a fraud. It is a cover-up of the ghastly and grizzly destruction of a marine environment by shipping firms and big oil companies.
There are solutions, Mr. Speaker, but this panel is simply spraying whitewash on the hull of a rusty supertanker on a collision course. The Prime Minister is Canada's version of Captain Hazelwood.

Mr. Speaker, last week, a number of Canadians received a questionnaire as part of a public opinion survey on the environment, sent by the Canadian Wildlife Federation.
Mr. Speaker, I think we all agree that this organization is doing veiy important and very good work.
However, in question No. 12, Canadians are asked to identify five areas on which the Canadian Wildlife Federation should focus in 1989. One of the fourteen areas listed is the following: "Impact of the Free Trade Agreement on the environment".
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what impact the Free Trade Agreement could have and indeed what connection it might have with the environment, since we know very well that the free trade agreement is about trade. The Federation must have made a mistake. I think it is useful to point out that there is a difference between the environment and the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Since the return of Parliament last Monday, both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport have repeatedly refused to refer the Prime Minister's decision to scrap VIA Rail to the Commons transport committee or to the National Transportation Agency. The Prime Minister will know that the Commons transport committee voted almost unanimously this morning to conduct public hearings on the government's plans to terminate VIA Rail.
October 3, 1989
Hear, hear!

Six of seven government members voted with the opposition in determining that there ought to be public hearings.
Will the Prime Minister now do the honourable thing and table the government's recommendations on the future of VIA Rail and immediately impose a moratorium on the implementation of those recommendations until the public hearings are conducted by the Commons transport committee and a report laid before the House for consideration by Parliament?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the reference levels respecting VIA Rail and other operations were contained in the budget that was tabled last April.
Clearly, there would be nothing at all, given the parliamentary reform that we introduced, that would have prevented the transport committee of the House of Commons to begin last April to consider any changes that they might have anticipated, or otherwise. This is part and parcel of the concept of parliamentary reform that I as Prime Minister am honoured to have introduced in this House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

My friend refers to-I think I am quoting him properly-"the Prime Minister's decision to scrap VIA Rail". He may want to wait for a little while to find out whether that statement is accurate or is fundamentally wrong. Because, no doubt, once he receives the facts that would normally dictate his course of action. I would think that the prudent thing for the member to do would be to wait for the decision of the government which will be announced shortly by the Minister of Transport.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has just told the House that he is honoured to have introduced parliamentary reform.
Oral Questions
I would ask him to honour the spirit of parliamentary reform by giving the House a commitment today that because a parliamentary committee comprised of members of all three parties has voted nearly unanimously- has said that this item is important enough and urgent enough to warrant emergency public hearings-that he, the Prime Minister of Canada, will impose a moratorium on the cuts to be announced tomorrow or some time very soon, and that those cuts will not be implemented, either the route eliminations or the 3,000 lay-offs, until the public has had a chance to be heard before the Commons transport committee and the transport committee makes its report to the Parliament of Canada. That is the question.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the point of my hon. friend. I find it a little difficult to understand his indignation. He was a member of a government that wiped out 20 per cent of VIA Rail without so much as a by your leave to the House of Commons. So while I understand the point he is trying to make, I would ask him to cool the indignation because it is really not going to go over in Canada.
With respect to our obligations to manage the government pursuant to the levels that are set out in the budget, this is precisely what we will do. Any parliamentarian or any parliamentary committee is free, of course, to take a look at the proposals of the government.
Our fundamental obligation to the people of Canada and to the Parliament of Canada is to manage the affairs of the nation in such a way as to bring about a much better economic situation, greater economic growth and better jobs for Canada in a more competitive economy. That is precisely what we are going to do. The budgetary implications are an important part of that plan.
So, if my hon. friend or members of the House wish to examine this, they will of course do so, I am sure very enthusiastically. But the Government of Canada is responsible for the conduct of the economic affairs of the nation. We shall implement these decisions and accept the verdict of Canadians at an appropriate time.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the Commons transport committee wants to examine a live VIA, not a dead carcass, which is what will happen unless the Prime Minister imposes a moratorium.
The lesson from Panama this morning is that those who do not respect parliamentary traditions eventually get the boot. The Prime Minister should pay attention.
I repeat my question to the Prime Minister. This morning, members of Parliament specifically charged with the responsibility of overseeing transportation policy in this Parliament, members of the transport committee from all three parties voted to hold public hearings on the future of VIA Rail because they regard the proposed cuts as an urgent matter requiring emergency public sessions.
If the Prime Minister is going to be consistent, if there is a need to allow the Commons finance committee to hold public hearings before proceeding on the goods and services tax, then surely there is a need to allow the Commons transport committee to hold public hearings before proceeding to slash VIA Rail.
Will the Prime Minister give that commitment today, or admit that his commitment to parliamentary reform is hypocrisy in the extreme?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have done nothing at all that would prevent any committee of this House from being seized of a proposed government course of action, holding hearings and making whatever decisions and recommendations they would like. In point of fact-
Before you act.

If my hon. friend will wait for the answer-as I have indicated, the reference levels were spelled out very clearly in the budget documents of April 27. At that very moment the committees of the House could have been meeting to examine any proposed course of action.
My hon. friend says the cut is an emergency. Well, any proposed compression budgegtaires is viewed by the opposition as an emergency because they have been so used to overspending that they do not understand that the time has come for some sanity in the public finances of Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Prime Minister. Canadians will find it hard to see how a parliamentary committee could study the future of VIA Rail before it has the details of the government's plans. There is some logic missing here. The Minister of National Revenue has said the government is going to spend more than $200 million a year and hire more than 5,000 tax police, one for every 300 taxpayers, to help collect the government's new goods and services tax.
I want to ask the Prime Minister, therefore, how can he justify hiring these 5,000 tax police, if he is concerned about government expenditure, and at the same time he is firing thousands of people at VIA Rail. Why doesn't he scrap the new goods and services tax and save VIA Rail?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mandate of this government is to make the country a more efficient place to live in as we look toward the future. That is what tax reform, including the move from the existing federal sales tax to the GST, is all about. It is so that future generations can reach their full potential in being able to create jobs and productivity in this country.
In the last four or five months our department has looked everywhere to utilize existing facilities. In order to dispel the figures that have been floating around- those of between 10,000 and 12,000 person years to administer GST-we have been able to bring that figure down to somewhere between 3,400 to 3,900 additional person years in order to provide a service for the taxpayer, particularly the small business community in this country, to make it easier for them to prepare for a smooth launch in 1991.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a strange vision of efficiency, hiring nearly 5,000 more public servants as tax inspectors and spending $1 billion over five years.

It is a strange vision of efficiency.
October 3, 1989

I want to ask the Prime Minister how many of these new tax police will be stationed in barber shops, and taxi cabs, How long will Canadians tolerate this government's spending $1 billion over five years to hire these new tax police to enforce a tax that Canadians don't want? Right on!

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. According to him, it was the responsibility of the Minister of Transport. My question is quite straightforward: Did the Minister of Transport do this kind of study?

Mr. Speaker, there is of course very close co-operation between the Department of Transport and the Department of the Environment on all matters that concern our two departments, on an ongoing basis. As for VIA Rail, I said yesterday that when the Government's decision was announced, we would release a number of comments or decisions regarding various subjects, and at that point the
Oral Questions
environment would be discussed, and I would advise the Leader of the New Democratic Party to wait for the Government's decision. Then and only then will we discuss the environmental issues.

Mr. Speaker, some comments are one thing. A comprehensive study is another. I want to address this question to the Minister of the Environment or the Minister of Transport.
In the election last year their boss, the Prime Minister, said:
We are prepared to subject every federal undertaking and every
undertaking on federal lands to a full environmental impact study.
Was there a full environmental impact study done about the possible closure of VIA? Yes or no. Is the government going to live up to its promises in this area. Yes or no.

Mr. Speaker, I said before that any decision dealing with VIA Rail would have to await the announcement. How can we say at the present time, today, that nothing or something will be done about VIA Rail when the decision is not known?

Mr. Speaker, I will try again. The question concerns the relationship between a comprehensive environmental impact study and the government's decision on VIA Rail. Government, dearly in the words of the Prime Minister last fall, in the words of the Minister of the Environment at the end of January of this year, indicated that before a major economic decision is taken in each and every case an environmental impact study will be undertaken and, if necessary, if the environmental conclusion leads to a negative result for this economic decision the environmental concerns would predominate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, clearly the leader of the NDP is not familiar with the federal process on the assessment of the environment.

Vancouver, Windsor, Quebec City, and Saint John, New Brunswick already have the worst ozone problems in Canada. Last year federal ozone guidelines were shattered 157 times in Toronto, and 189 times in Windsor.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government and my department have made sure in all circumstances that the environmental review process has been respected in every phase. This is the same in all the megaprojects. Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is quite right when he points to the excellent record that we have had in reducing the size of the public service by 12,000 people. In so doing, we have reduced the overhead of the Government of Canada by 10 per cent from what it was in 1984-85. Clearly our record speaks for itself.
My colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, has said that for the new goods and services tax we will need additional resources. He has spoken clearly as to what those resources will be.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Government of Canada in Cambodia is to contribute to a circumstance in which the Cambodian people themselves can decide their own futures.
I listened with interest to the hon. member's personal view that the Hun Sen regime enjoys the widespread support of the people of Cambodia. That is far from clear. There has been a Vietnamese withdrawal. That Vietnamese withdrawal is due in part to the fact that Canada, other western countries, and our allies in ASEAN maintained a very strong position over the last several years. We think this is not the time to break that kind of strong position. No one wants anything to do with Pol Pot or the Pol Pot faction of the Khmer Rouge regime. The reality is that the Khmer Rouge commands authority in Cambodia.
When we have been looking, as we did actively through the Paris Peace Conference this summer, for a means by which there could be a coalition government or an interim authority that could speak for all of the Cambodian people we were seeking to minimize the role of the Khmer Rouge.
I can assure the hon. member that I have been following this matter with our allies closely, including most recently in discussions with the foreign ministers of the other members of the G-7 in New York on Thursday night.
