speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today the House is being asked to consider a bill to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. Programs under these pieces of legislation have provided producers of storable crops with interest-free guaranteed loans at harvest time.
Government Orders
The amended legislation, as set out in the bill, will maintain loan guarantees for advance payments that will help promote the orderly marketing of agricultural commodities in this country. Farmers will still be able to obtain the financing they need to carry crops from harvest time to delivery. That means that they can continue to take advantage of marketing opportunities and that seasonal price fluctuations can be smoothed out. Under the Crops Act the advances are administered through producer organizations which have entered into agreements with the federal government. This year we have agreements with 55 such organizations. The advance is extended to the farmer by the producer organization and is repaid by the farmer when the crop is delivered. The government guarantees these advances against default by farmers so that their organization and lenders take no risk.
Under the act covering prairie grains, advances are extended by Canadian Wheat Board through elevator companies. The loans are repaid through deductions on payments received by farmers when the grain is delivered. Again in this case, the government guarantees these loans. Neither the Canadian Wheat Board nor the lenders are at risk. Over the summer, consultations with producer organizations have enabled us to put forward this amending legislation with a number of improvements to the legislation that was originally introduced. I want to thank hon. members for their co-operation in allowing that bill to be withdrawn and to be replaced with this one which incorporates a number of those improvements.
To provide better security the acts will guarantee the payment of interest as well as the advance. If a producer is in default, both the principle and any accumulated interest will be covered. As well, any producer organization that administers the advances is accountable for 10 per cent of defaults on principle and interest on an individual basis up to an aggregate of 2 per cent of all advances made by it.
The Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act will be further amended so that interest rates will be designated by the minister, rather than by regulation. This is already the case as provided for in the Advance Payments for Crops Act. This change will help get advance payments

Government Orders
into the hands of producers more quickly. In addition, the advance limits would be designated by the minister each year up to a level of $250,000. Many producer organizations have requested such action. Previous limits were set at $30,000 for an individual producer; $60,000 for a partnership of two; and $90,000 for a corporation of three or more producers.
These limits were established to control interest costs to the government, but since the government is no longer paying these costs, we can remove these statutory limits and establish new limits set by the Minister of Agriculture.
I would also like to take note here that the Advance Payments for Crops Act is being amended to include oats. We have taken this action since prairie oats are no longer being marketed through the Canadian Wheat Board.
Under the legislation that we are considering today, farmers will still be able to obtain the credit they need to hold crops off the market for whatever period they choose. The principal change is that they will now have to pay interest on the loans taken out. This means that the decision to sell or hold their crop will be based on business principles rather than on the availability of an interest-free loan.
Interest rates will be based on rates negotiated by the Canadian Wheat Board or the producer organizations with the lending institutions. These rates will be significantly lower than what otherwise would be the case if producers or their organizations sought credit independently of these federally secured programs. Farmers acting on their own would generally pay rates anywhere from one to three percentage points higher than that which will be negotiated. It is normal practice for farmers to carry some crop inventories past harvest. Delivery schedules may be staggered or farmers may anticipate that prices will improve later in the year, or it could be to their advantage to delay crop receipts to the next year. These are business decisions and interest charges associated with carrying inventories are expenses regularly faced by Canadian business.
The amendments to the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act will save Canadian taxpayers and the federal treasury about $20 million this fiscal year. Over the next four years the savings will total $100 million.
Everyone is being asked to contribute to deficit reduction. In this case, in a modest way, the Government of Canada is asking the farmers of Canada to contribute in a small way.
Since the government assumed office we have been successful in reducing the deficit from a level of $38 billion in 1984, when we came into office, to a level of $28.7 billion in the last fiscal year, a reduction of almost $10 billion. It is a painful process and it is not easy.
As well, we have slowed the rate of growth of the debt from 24 per cent a year, which was occurring before we came into office in 1984, to a level of less than 10 per cent per year. As the Minister of Finance has indicated, we have reduced the size and the cost of the administration of government. We have reduced the size of the public service. We have taken a number of expenditure reduction measures all in the interest of bringing our revenues and expenditures more into line.
Despite these best efforts, the debt is still outstripping our ability to carry it.
Don't forget the huge tax increases.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is why my colleague, the Minister of Finance, has this past April prescribed some very tough measures in which all Canadians are being asked to share, measures which include this provision which all together will reduce the deficit to approximately $15 billion by 1993 and 1994.
I heard the hoii. member say, "Don't forget about the taxes". Well, it really invites me to say something about the Liberal debt that this government inherited, a debt of $200 billion.
What is it now?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what is it now? I am glad the member asked that. It is about $350 billion, and the $150 billion is interest on the debt that we inherited in 1984. We have not added one plug nickel to the nation's debt on the basis of program expenditures.
You have been in power five years.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What we have been left with is a legacy, a mountain of debt which Canadians are now being asked to service and for which Canadians are being asked to sacrifice. Hon. members can chirp over there all they like. It is not our debt, it is their debt. Unfortunately all Canadians have to pay for their mistakes.
October 3, 1989
You have doubled the debt in a mere five years.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Since the fiscal year of 1987-88, our budgetary revenues have exceeded our program expenditures in each and every year. What has been killing us is the cost of servicing the Liberal debt. It is a Liberal debt and it is a Liberal legacy and Canadians will never forget that.
Oh, oh!
You have raised taxes 30 times.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, all Canadians and even Liberals are going to have to face up to this. We must build for the future. We must reduce the debt. We cannot continue to borrow from the future and that is what this piece of legislation addresses. I know that hon. members opposite will oppose it because they have been so used to spending like drunken sailors that they will not take charge of the situation and we have got to take charge.
While these budgetary cuts will have some impact upon the farm sector, it does not in any way suggest that the Government of Canada is walking away from supporting the farmers of Canada. We have a distinguished record in terms of what we have done in the past.
Federal government support for agriculture has been unprecedented since we have come to office in 1984. Direct federal support to Canadian agriculture totalled some $6 billion in 1987-88. Whether it has been drought, whether it has been grasshoppers, whether it has been floods, or whether it has been depressed commodity prices, this government has been there to respond to the needs of the farmers, and we will continue to do that.
We are asking the agriculture sector to do its share and to help overcome Canada's deficit problems. Farmers, like other Canadians, in the long run will benefit from the action we are taking today to put this country on a sounder financial footing. The changes necessitated by the budget must go forward and that is why we are bringing this legislation forward today.
Government Orders
Yes, the producers will have to pay interest, but the guarantees offered them through their producer organizations will allow them to get the cash they need at a better rate of interest.
I know now that the issue is not the interest rate question as much as the fact that what is needed is the enabling legislation so farmers can go out and apply for cash advances under the provisions of this legislation. So there is, indeed, some urgency to the passage of this legislation.
The acts will still help producers store crops after harvest in order to market them later, and this means more reasonable prices at harvest time for other producers and a better average price throughout the year. Advance payments legislation will, as I said, continue to provide significant benefits to Canadian producers and I would urge the members on all sides of the House to consider the urgency of this so that farmers can, indeed, apply for advances and receive those advances in order to make their marketing decisions and in order to calculate their cash flow in an orderly fashion.

Madam Speaker, the minister has certainly outlined the purpose of this bill, a bill that was introduced in the House of Commons back in the late 1950s by the Diefenbaker government. There is no doubt the government of the time had a lot of foresight and recognized the need for legislation such as this, whereby a farmer could borrow money against the crops that are in storage, interest free money that helped tailor the supply of food to market.
I feel bad that the present day members of that party have lost sight of that need, and have lost sight of the need of the farmers particularly in a year like this when harvests were delayed across the northern part of the Prairies with the result that the grades of those crops have deteriorated to the point where they will not return as much to the producer as they would in a normal year.
I take part in this debate today in the hope that the government will reconsider its current trend of abandoning the Canadian farmers. This bill is another example of the complete disregard of this government for our major primary industry, and it is the latest in a series of moves that is throwing Canadian farmers to the vultures of the market-place, a market-place that has been racked by investigations and scandals and charges of insider trading in some commodity exchanges.

Government Orders
Back in July of 1985, the headlines of the London Free Press stated "Ottawa Kisses Off The Family Farm". I had hoped they were wrong because I am a farmer at heart. My son is a farmer. However, when we look at events since then we realize that they were correct. We have seen a grape industry ravaged. A healthy tobacco industry, with the highest quality and the lowest chemical content of any in the world, has been partially destroyed. The two-price wheat system was discontinued in spite of a 1986 recommendation of $10 per bushel for wheat consumed domestically.
We were assured the marketing boards were not on the bargaining table at the free trade negotiations, yet these boards, particularly in the poultry sector, were gutted. Look at what was done with chicken, for example. There are 13 different types of further processed chicken that are no longer classified to be chicken, nine different types of turkey which are not considered to be turkeys that will be allowed into Canada through the Free Trade Agreement and will enter without restriction. The Canadian people and the Canadian farmers now realize who are the real turkeys, the ones who negotiated this agreement. This systematic dismantling of our Canadian farm programs is destroying the Canadian family farm, not by a direct frontal attack but by a series of attacks on the superstructures of the industry. Apparently the government seems to think that agriculture is just another big business. It seems to think if you can produce iron ore cheaper in South America, we can do the same with foods.
The farmers of this nation will never accept the living conditions of those in the Third World countries. They demand better, and if we are expected to compete against the multinational companies that control the world's grain trade we must continue our programs that have made Canadian farmers among the most efficient in the world, who produce the highest quality grains in the world and do it through the marketing systems that we have in place and programs like those that are being gutted here today.
I have to ask the government why it did not raise this hidden agenda four years ago instead of the piece-bypiece dismantling that we have been witnessing since that time. Let us take the Farm Credit Corporation, for example. The 1988-89 corporate plan was tabled late,
late in the evening just before we adjourned for Christmas. Of course when we look back, we realize it had to be done after the election, but not seven months late.
Then, of course, the annual report of the Farm Credit Corporation for 1988-89 was due in early June and tabled late on the night we adjourned June 27.
Then we had the cabinet directive to the Farm Credit Corporation of July 1988 that was not tabled even though by law it should have been tabled within the next 15 sitting days of Parliament. The government is treating the members of Parliament like mushrooms that you keep in the dark and feed on a special diet. If the government intends to phase out the Farm Credit Corporation, it should tell us and tell the farmers of Canada because we have to know. Please stop the discrimination of requiring farmers in some provinces to sign covenants that are illegal in other provinces and are not being treated equally.
There are provisions under section ll(l)(e) of the Farm Credit Corporation Act to make compositions, schemes of arrangement, re-writing of mortgages, etc., but it was never the intent of the legislators that we should go so far as to force these people to sign away their future, their heart and their souls. I call on the government to stop these practices, to accept the responsibility and realize that Canadian agriculture cannot be run like big corporations. When one examines some of the actions of the Farm Credit Corporation and looks at some of the situations, one has to realize that at this time it is as much a collection agency as it is a lending agency.
I want to commend the representatives of the four churches for their involvement a week ago yesterday on behalf of Canadian farm families.
This government is slowly but surely dismantling the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Growers Marketing Board. When the levels of subsidy are at an equal level there must be free movement of grain according to the free trade deal. This means that probably by late next year we will see cheaper and lower quality United States grains-I am referring here to wheat and barley-coming into Canada and undermining our price structures and quality standards. In fact, the end users certificates that will accompany this grain will not even show the quality or grade of product.
October 3, 1989

The travesty of this situation is that processors can bring in a few loads of low quality grain and undermine a price structure here in Canada of the high quality Canadian grain, all at the expense of Canadian producers. If this government is going to be the frontman for big business, and if the rural roots are cut off, this primary industry will wither and die.
We have come to be known around the world as a land of plenty, but when I look at what is happening to the resource sector of this country and how this government has allowed these areas to be decimated, I realize that this will impact not just on our present generation of Canadians and our farmers, but also future generations of Canadians and the nation.
Let me give you a few examples. Fishing is a resource industry and on both coasts it is in difficulty. Stocks are depleted on the east coast by overfishing, plants are closing and people have been thrown out of work. On the west coast we lost the dispute requiring Canadian fish to be processed at Canadian plants and our fish farms are being sold to foreign interests.
Our lumber industry has been devastated by the Free Trade Agreement. In 1986, we had over one-third of the total U.S. market. Now we have about one-quarter.
Our oil industry is suffering its worst year in terms of oil wells drilled and completed. This is another resource sector.
The number of oil wells that were brought into production as of the end of September was approximately 1,200. Let us compare that to what has happened in the past. In 1983 that number was 2,606. In 1984 it was 3,900. In 1985 it was 4,723, four times as many as this year. In September, 1989, there were only 157 drilling rigs working in Canada, while 342 were sitting idle. There are only two rigs drilling in all of northern Canada, and none in the offshore. This is a major resource industry and the policies of the government have virtually shut down the oil industry in Canada.
My point is that these resource industries create much of the nation's new wealth and create the basic production from which the growth of our economy emanates and the spin-off from these new wells spreads to the manufacturing sector, the service sector and the total economy. I submit that the health of these resource sectors reflects through the rest of the economy and the whole nation will eventually suffer from the impact.
Government Orders
No nation such as Canada should ever allow itself to become dependent on others for food, particularly a great nation like Canada whose potential is tempered only by climate and distances to markets.
The original bill was designed-the original bill that we are debating here today and which has been in effect for so many years and served us so well-was designed to allow these farmers to store their crops and feed them into the market as the need arose. I want to use this as an example. Many tobacco farmers used this original bill and it worked very well. Normally in the tobacco industry the money was only needed for three or four months, from harvest time until the crop was sold at producer-run or auction exchanges.
When I look at the new bill, we have to check and see if there is an advantage to producers. I worked this through on a $30,000 loan to a tobacco farmer for four months. Using the new legislation, because the farmer will be charged interest, it works out that the farmer will have an advantage of about $45. That will not even cover his costs for paperwork and bookkeeping.
The minister was asking us a few moments ago if we as farmers would do our part to bring down the deficit. I have to submit that we are doing our part and I will bring that out in a few minutes.
Another area where this is going to hit extremely hard is where it will take cash out of the pockets of the farmer. Certainly as we look at the areas of environmental concern and stewardship of our soil, if a farmer is expected to do his part, why is this government so insistent on slashing our programs? I suggest the whole cost of environmental and soil management programs will fall on the farmer's shoulders as the margins of return on investment, management and labour are already pared to the bone.
I respectfully suggest this latest move will impact on our environment and soil conservation efforts because of the additional cost to the farmer of this particular piece of legislation, Bill C-36. This bill is another example of producer abandonment. I call on the minister to reinstate this bill to its previous form and intent or to withdraw it completely. This bill will force producers who are in a financial bind to sell their grain at harvest time in order to get cash to pay the production costs. We do not have to be financial wizards to know what happens to the price at market time when the farmers are forced to sell.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders
Let me give a few examples of what this program will mean to the producer in terms of stabilizing a price over the period the grain is in storage. I will use com as an example. These are figures from the Ontario Com Growers Association. In 1986-1987, the average increased value per tonne from storage was $4.54; in 1987-1988, that same advantage for storing that product and releasing it into the market at a later date was $36.30 per tonne, money that is sorely needed by the producers and this legislation has to be made available to them.
The government is making these cuts on the pretext of cutting expenditures when in fact it is biting the hand that feeds it. The total cost of this program is approximately $20 million to $25 million, maybe $27 million. Yet the government will take in about $995 million, almost $1 billion, in tax on alcoholic beverages. That is the increase in this year's budget.
Even more ludicrous is the fact that these fellows who take $1.8 billion in taxes from the tobacco industry are now withdrawing a program in this sector of the industry that costs the government $1 million. That is quite a return on the investment. The tobacco industry is contributing $1.8 billion and it is only costing the government $1 million. I think the government should reassess its position and withdraw this legislation.
How can this government be so callous? The projected taxes from the tobacco industry are as I just have stated. Add on alcoholic beverages of $995 million, plus an additional increase of $700 million in the sales tax on these items in this year's budget for a total of $3.5 billion from tobacco and alcohol alone and the total budget of the department is $2.35 billion in the coming year.
This reminds me of some of the earlier medical practices where a patient got sick and the early doctors of the day would bleed them a little bit. Of course, if they didn't get better, you bled them a little bit more. That is what the symptoms are here today. I should remind the government that quite often the patients died.
I submit that the discontinuation of these interest free loans and the dismantling of various other programs will mean the death of Canadian family farms because they are already being bled to death.
A few moments ago I spoke about some of the tactics of the Farm Credit Corporation on withholding reports and directives. Thousands of Canadian farmers and their families are in arrears with the FCC. This will further multiply the problem because they are counting on these interest free loans to tide them over.
Recently a constituent of mine received notice of order of sale just before he was to start harvesting his soybean and com. At a time when he had a cash flow that was going to be available to him within a month or six weeks, this happened to him. I think that we should reassess what is happening with Farm Credit. It has become more of a collection agency than a lending agency.
I mentioned a moment ago that the amount of feed grade wheat is above normal. Consequently, the average price to the producer will be down dramatically. These interest free loans are needed and they are needed now, or else the number of farmers who will be foreclosed on will increase in the next few months.
It seems strange indeed that at the same time the government is cutting back on Canadian producers, the United States producers of soybeans in particular are already pressuring their government to bring in a similar program to stop the exploitation by the very large corporations and the speculators in the commodity exchanges.
In fact, if the Canadian program is being looked at as a subsidy by the U.S., has our government not challenged them on the Commodity Credit Corporation loans or the Export Enhancement Corporation loans? I wonder if the government got assurances from the U.S. that it will bring an immediate end to its export enhancement programs that drive down the price of international grains. The government is forging ahead with this legislation that will create additional hardship on our people.
I have a whole series of letters and requests from various producer organizations across Canada. One is dated October 2 from Prairie Pools Incorporated asking the government not to proceed with this bill. There is
October 3, 1989

another one from a meeting held in Winnipeg yesterday. Several farm organizations asked the government to withdraw this legislation. There are representations from all across Canada on this particular piece of legislation by producers' organizations asking us to put a stop to this madness and to leave the legislation in place which has served us well over the years.
Therefore, I move:
That Bill C-36 be amended by removing all of the words after the
word "That" and by substituting the following:
"this House declines to proceed with Bill C-36, An Act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act because it opposes in principle, namely, the elimination of interest free loans to producer organizations and producers".
This motion is seconded by the Hon. Member for Algoma.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair has received the amendment and it will be taken under advisement as to its admissibility. I will return to the House later with a ruling on it.

Madam Speaker, it is always a pleasure to stand in this House and debate the great issues of the day, but it is certainly not a pleasure to have to stand up in the House and discuss what is happening to agriculture as a result of the bill that is before us.
It seems that every time I stand here as the member for Prince Albert, I have another reason to remember my predecessor, the former member for Prince Albert, the late John George Diefenbaker. It was my predecessor who in 1957 saw the very obvious need for this kind of legislation and brought it in to great acclaim on the prairies. In fact, that measure was so popular that in the 1958 election, even people who were normally CCF voters supported the Chief because of what he was doing for prairie farmers.
I think it is a real shame that this government, made up of members of the late John George Diefenbaker's party, have turned its back on so many of the legacies that John left behind.
Government Orders
It is doubly unfortunate because it was prairie members and farm members of the Conservative party who got elected on the legacy of John Diefenbaker who in fact kept the Conservative party alive through its years in the wilderness. Now that it has become a government, suddenly it is quite fashionable to forget about the farmers who kept that party alive through the years.
There are a number of reasons why I oppose this bill, one of which certainly is that farmers do not need any more interest-bearing debts. I listened very carefully, or tried to, to what the minister was saying. There were three reasons that he gave, as I understood it, for introducing the bill at this time. One was that there is a real sense of urgency, that we need to get cash advances out into the hands of farmers. Certainly that is true. The crop is largely off in many parts of the country. Certainly it is off in our part of the country. People have been counting on that money, but have not not been able to get it. All of us from rural constituencies have had phone calls, letters and so on asking:"When will the cash advances will be available?".
However, that is no real cause for urgency at all because until this bill is passed, the old bill remains in effect. In fact, if the government had been so anxious to get money into the hands of farmers, it could very well have done it under the old legislation. That in fact is what many farmers across the country have asked the government to do. Therefore there is no urgency at all, other than that imposed by the government itself in passing this legislation at this time.
The second reason that the hon. minister gave, as I understood it, was the need to cope with the deficit. I want to ask the minister, is there not a real cost involved in continuing the cycle of increasing debt, farm foreclosure and rural depopulation? Surely there is a real cost involved in loss of infrastructure, loss of taxes and the cost of relocating all those people and providing goods and services to them in new places when they are forced off the farms into towns and cities across the country. There is a real cost involved in that. All too often those kinds of costs are not figured into this government's equation.
Third, surely when making decisions like this for financial reasons, there should be a careful measurement of the costs and benefits of such a move. The figures that the hon. member who spoke previously alluded to from the Ontario Com Producers indicate clearly what a cost- effective program this has been.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders
For example, the figures produced by the Ontario Com Producers show that in 1986, the value of this program to com producers was $2,044,826, but at a cost to the treasury of only $1,175,976. It was even much more dramatic in 1987-88 when the Ontario Com Producers realized a net benefit of $16,000,796 at a cost to the treasury of only $1,121,000. That is a ratio of $15 to $1. For every dollar invested by the government, there is a return to the farmers in net benefit of $15. Surely that is one of the best expenditures this government has ever made. At least I have not seen any better.
The last point with regard to the deficit is that there is a real contradiction involved in the approach of the minister when he says that it is absolutely essential that we save this $27 million and at the same time he brags about the fact that the government has spent $6 billion on agriculture over the last number of years. Surely this is not such a big percentage of $6 billion that it is absolutely critical to wipe it out in that kind of a context.
I think what really got to the point of this whole issue was when the minister indicated that introducing this bill and making farmers pay interest on the cash advances will permit farmers to make decisions based on business principles. That is a very short-sighted and narrow view of what business principles involve. To me, it shows a total lack of understanding of how the whole grain marketing and collection system in this country actually works.
Surely there are important business principles involved in things like orderly marketing. Surely there are business principles involved in being able to store grain and put it on to the market to counter the price cycles so that farmers can sell their grain or their produce when the prices are high rather than when the prices are low. Surely there is a cost to the whole system if that system that has been built up over the last 50 years is suddenly destroyed and we have no other system to take its place.
Let me explain in a little more detail how that works. The way the cash advance program works is that in effect farmers can sell their grain when they take it off. As soon as the crop is in the bin, they are able to get an interest free cash advance and they in effect have sold that grain at that point. That is very important because our grain handling system, at least in western Canada, can only
absorb 40 per cent of the annual production of the prairies at any one time.
The whole system in western Canada can only absorb 40 per cent of the grain at any one time. It means that the grain has to cycle through that system two and a half times in the course of a year in order to move all the grain, and the same I understand is true in other parts of the country. That means it is in fact not possible for farmers to make decisions, as the minister would imply, solely on the basis of price because there is not enough capacity to do so.
Over the years we have introduced a very effective system that is the envy of farmers all over the world and that is a quota system which allows the Canadian Wheat Board, for example, or the Ontario Wheat Board to make sales in advance and know what kind of supplies it is getting and be able to call those supplies into the system at the time when it can be shipped.
There is no point, there is no benefit, there is no business advantage to all the grain that is produced in a year being dumped into the system all at once. It has to be sorted into train loads and into terminals and on to ships and so on. It makes a heck of a lot more business sense, as far as I am concerned, to call that grain forward at the time that it can move all the way through the system very quickly, through the local elevators, through the railway system, through the terminals and on to the boats.
Surely an efficient modem system is something we have had a lot of debate about in the House, or other members have, I being new here, debate about how we have to enhance the ability to move grain very quickly through the system in response to demand. This bill effectively undermines that capacity.
It would perhaps be a different situation if we were making moves to increase the handling capacity of the system, but we are not. Our whole emphasis in the last 15 years has been on moving it through quicker with reduced storage facilities. At the time when this legislation was originally introduced, the elevator system was able to handle about 50 per cent to 55 per cent of the grain at any one time. Now it is down to 40 per cent. That 40 per cent is being rapidly eroded by the whole process of elevator rationalization and rail line abandonment which certainly is another related issue.
October 3, 1989

The government, at the same time that it cut the cash advance program in the last budget, also cut all funds to the rail branch line rehabilitation program. In my own constituency of Prince Albert-Churchill River there are two lines, the Blaine Lake subdivision between Shellbrook and Blaine Lake, and the Paddockwood subdivision which serves the points of Henribourg and Paddockwood. Those are million bushel points. The elevator companies there are perfectly prepared to keep on handling grain up to the year 2000 or beyond because they are viable points. Everybody assumed that this government was going to stick to the commitments it made regularly, that that system which had been included in the year 2000 system would in fact be upgraded.
On these rail lines, the roadbeds were rebuilt, there was new ballast and there were new ties. All they lacked was heavy steel. But this government, by its budget moves, has made it impossible to get that heavy steel down so now there is a threat for those three-million bushel points to be abandoned in the next short period of time.
That kind of a situation is duplicated right across the prairies, which means that we will have even less than 40 per cent capacity in the system. That means that there is an even greater need to call grain forward in an orderly fashion to take advantage of the new rapid through-put kind of system that we are obviously developing.
The second point is that this really starts to open up wide cracks in the whole quota system that has been so successful in this country. We have been able to maintain the kind of marketing system, the Canadian Wheat Board, which I think everybody concedes has maximized benefits to producers far beyond what any other grain handling system in the world has been able to do. Certainly that is the opinion of the vast majority of farmers on the prairies.
That quota system will be very effectively undermined because when producers face the prospect of not being able to haul in all their grain or not being able to get interest free cash advances on their grain, they are going to put all kinds of pressure on to be able to haul that grain all at once. Why, because of lack of capacity in the system, should one farmer be able to haul his grain in
Government Orders
September and pay his bills and the next one in December, the next one in March, the next one in June? It is not possible for everybody to do it at once, so there is going to be real pressure exerted from all kinds of grassroots farmers who need that money very badly to start to eliminate the quota system which has been at the foundation of our grain handling and transportation systems.
I guess what amazes me as well is the whole lack of consultation that is characteristic of this government's approach to agriculture. As I mentioned before, this party opposite was kept alive and nurtured through its bleaker years by the farmers of Canada. Farmers assumed that when this government came to office, certainly its policies toward agriculture would be undertaken with the widest possible consultation and that they would have friends in government. How often have we seen that that is not true? Once again that is not true, because, as the previous speaker mentioned, there have been representations from all over the country objecting very strongly to this legislation.
The Advisory Committee to the Canadian Wheat Board, certainly an important policy body on the prairies, wrote to the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds last July 13 offering him the unanimous resolution that the Advisory Committee to the Canadian Wheat Board recommend to the federal government that for the 1989-90 crop year the cash advance program be operated as it was in the 1988-89 crop year.
In passing that motion, the committee noted that it also wanted to give recognition to the fact that economic factors continue to create serious financial stress for many producers in western Canada. I can vouch for that being true. I have spoken to many farmers in my constituency and throughout northern Saskatchewan in the last several weeks and months.
Although the yield is not as bad as it was last year because there were better rains, though there was a period of drought and certainly the grains are just awful, there is a large quantity of feed wheat in the system, wheat that is worth only half of what people had expected to get. There is not only the outstanding debt from previous years, but that debt is not going to be dealt with at all in this coming year because of the very poor grades that so much of the wheat came in at.

Government Orders
The National Farmers Union wrote in mid August that a cash advance program is urgently needed for the 1989-90 crop year since farmers need cash flow now to pay their bills.
The prairie pools say that the changes will hurt orderly marketing and undermine the Canadian Wheat Board because it will be more difficult to manage deliveries.
Manitoba's Keystone Agriculture Producers noted a very special situation. It said that the elimination of the interest free provision under both acts would be particularly onerous for grains and oilseeds producers in Manitoba who are virtually obliged to ship their commodities through the port at Thunder Bay. Because that port is closed during the winter months, in contrast to Vancouver and Prince Rupert, many farmers in Manitoba sit all winter with little or no opportunity to market grain, resulting in turn in their having little income with which to pay their bills and support the economies of their local communities.
Certainly I would expect that there are a fair number of government members representing Manitoba farmers. I would hope that they had drawn this very directly to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds who, ironically, is himself a farmer in Manitoba and should know very well what the effect would be on Manitoba.
The letter that I found most interesting, however, dated August 2 and arrived by fax, is addressed to the Prime Minister of Canada and reads:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,
At a national meeting held in Winnipeg this morning, 19 Canadian grain and oilseed producer organizations were unanimous in calling on your government to withdraw Bill C-36, and to re-institute the two previous acts, which provided for interest-free cash advances, for crops grown in Canada.
In our view, Bill C-36 will destroy the value of the Cash Advance Programs.
Your federal Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Mazankowski, has initiated a major review of agriculture policy in Canada, of which marketing is one aspect. We feel the Cash Advance Programs should be part of this review.
It is urgent to reinstate the 1988/89 Cash Advance Programs, and to allow the farm community with the federal minister, through the policy review process, to design the appropriate marketing systems to ensure equity in the system.
Yours truly,
Roy Cusitar Meeting Chairman
The interesting thing about this letter is not so much what it says but who signed it. People who have followed the agriculture debate over the years know that there is in some respect a bit of a polarization within the farm community between those who favour the orderly marketing approach, the pooling kind of approach, and those who prefer a more of a free open market kind of approach to agriculture. That tension has been very clear in debates like that on the Crow rate and so on.
This particular letter is signed by groups like the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association, Western Barley Growers Association, Alberta Pulse Growers Association, Focus on Inputs, Prairie Canola Growers Council, Manitoba Canola Growers Association, Saskatchewan Canola Growers Association, Alberta Soft Wheat Grain Association, United Grain Growers, Flax Council of Canada, Atlantic Grains Council, Ontario Com Producers Association, Manitoba Pulse Growers Association and Western Canada Pulse Growers Association.
What those who follow this debate closely will recognize immediately is that most of the signatures on this particular letter are from people who have historically supported an opening up of free market forces within agriculture. A good number of those groups in fact even supported the free trade initiatives, although there were groups that had misgivings, including the federations of agriculture, the pools and so on. The majority of signa-tors to this particular letter were in favour of the free trade deal and thought it would be a good deal for agriculture. This is the government's very own friends that it is turning its back on.
I would also like to comment briefly on the effect on individual farmers. When a farmer puts in a crop, that is largely done with borrowed money. Today's input costs are so high that there is no way that the vast majority of farmers have the cash on hand in spring when the crop goes in to pay for those input costs, so that crop is put in on credit. What has traditionally happened is that when the crop came off in September, October or November, in the fall, the farmer was then able to take an interest free cash advance, pay those debts and thus be rid of the interest charges on those debts through the rest of the year and, in fact, could manage a cash flow so that the planning process for the next spring could begin again.

What this bill does, by imposing interest charges on those farmers, is in fact make this a very unattractive option for farmers. Certainly I can appreciate that perhaps there would be a slight interest rate saving of 1 per cent or 2 per cent.
But when you are talking of interest rates of 13 or 14 per cent, and with the grab and steal tax coming in, we could well be looking at interest rates in the neighbourhood of 20 per cent. With the added inflation that particular tax measure could very well induce, and with the policy of John Crowe to raise interest rates to compensate for every rise in inflation we could well be looking at interest rates in the 20 per cent range again within a year or two. So farmers are going to save 1 per cent or 2 per cent in interest, but they are just going to get killed by the interest rates. If there is one thing that farmers do not need it is more interest bearing debt.
I would also like to talk a little bit about what this represents in the larger context of farm policy. What is becoming very frustrating, not only to members on this side of the House but to farmers across this country, and I suspect even to some of the government's own backbenchers, is this government's unwillingness to come clean with its real agenda on agriculture.
Within the last very short period of time we have seen a number of measures taken by this government that to me point very much in the same direction. We saw oats being removed from the Canadian Wheat Board's jurisdiction. This was, of course, supposed to be a big bonanza for farmers. As a result, there were much lower sales of oats at much lower prices this year than there had been in the past few years. So the bonanza never materialized.
People were skeptical about that whole maneuver to begin with. Something like 70 to 80 per cent of farmers called on the government to change its decision, not to introduce that Order in Council to take oats out of the wheat board's jurisdiction, including many friends of the government who I met at meetings who stood up and made their views known very forcefully. But oats were removed from the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. Certainly that led to the clear impression being left in the farm community that the Wheat Board was no longer the major instrument of government policies, if
Government Orders
you will, the sacrosanct institution of Canadian agriculture that it had once been. Certainly, removing the cash advances is another blow to that whole system.
Second, there is the whole question of free trade. Although the government spelled out, it seemed very directly, that free trade was not going to be a hindrance to agriculture and certainly was not going to have any impact on orderly marketing, a lot of producers were very dubious about that assertion. I suspect those numbers include the former Minister of Agriculture, the former minister from Elgin who, it is widely rumored, in fact chose not to run again in the last election because of what he feared was going to happen to the orderly marketing system which he strongly believed in. I know he did. I lived in that part of the country in the early 1970s and knew the former minister to be a strong supporter of orderly marketing. I think he just did not want to see what was going to be happening.
It has been argued that some of the things that have happened since the Free Trade Agreement, for example, the ruling by GATT on the import regulations on ice cream and yoghurt and the American countervail on pork, are not the result of free trade, that those kinds of things would have happened anyway. In a narrow sense that is perhaps true. However, I remember very clearly the Premier of Saskatchewan, one of the most ardent apologists, in fact one of the most ardent cheerleaders for this government's agricultural policy, coming to our city of Prince Albert and saying very directly to farmers who were concerned about these things that certainly it is not going to undermine orderly marketing. And even if the jots and tittles, as the Minister of Trade refers to them, do not necessarily spell out in every detail how orderly marketing is going to be protected, it is going to create a climate of harmony, it is going to create a climate of goodwill between the United States and Canada where the type of harassment that we had seen an increasing amount of was not going to be visible any longer.
That has clearly turned out to be only so much hot air, frankly. The harassment has not only not decreased, it has actually picked up, as evidenced by the very destructive ruling from GATT launched by a New York dairy producer and the recent ruling on pork.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders
As well, we saw under free trade the loss of the two-price wheat system. We were told that was going to be compensated for, and nowhere do I find in the government's financial plans for the future that that particular promise is going to be kept either.
Later this week we will debate again the bill that we gave second reading to under closure, the plant breeders' rights bill, again another bill that opens up the whole industry of agriculture, the whole farm community, to increasing threat from large corporations and increasing corporate control of that sector.
Then I had the pleasure, I guess, of attending the press conference in my own city of Prince Albert when the Minister of Agriculture and the provincial ministers of agriculture announced their new policy on agriculture. There were a couple of very key words in there that certainly anybody who follows agriculture debates heard very clearly, namely, that the new look of agriculture was to be; one, market-driven; and two, self-reliant. It is very easy to find words that to the average Canadian sound as if they represent progress. Who is going to be against markets? Well I guess some people are, but certainly nobody is against self-reliance.
What that obviously has come to mean in the context of the government's other activities is that the historic foundation of agriculture in this country, the family farm, is something that this government is perfectly willing to abandon. Every action this government takes in the field of agriculture makes that more and more clear.
I think family farmers are starting to realize that they are being abandoned, that they are being left behind, that this government is doing whatever it can to hasten the corporate concentration in agriculture, to hasten the industrialization of the agriculture sector. What is really frustrating is that farmers always feel like they are fighting rearguard actions because the government is saying one thing, that, yes, the family farm is sacred, and, yes, it is doing what it can to assist and support the family farm, but all the actions run the other way.
It is becoming very frustrating and very tiring for family farmers to constantly fight these rearguard actions against the government that will not come clean on what its actual agenda is. I am sure there are a lot of
members opposite, a lot of farm members in particular, who are starting to realize as well that what this government says is much different from what this government does.
In that regard I would like to offer some evidence that this frustration is not just something that comes out of what might be termed the left wing of the farm movement or out of the Official Opposition or the NDP. This whole frustration with the direction this government is taking in agriculture is shared every bit as much by its own members, its own grassroots members.
I would like to quote from The Western Producer, a paper with a circulation of approximately 130,000 a very important farm paper. My copy is a little bit worn by now because I have been showing it to all my colleagues from other parts of Canada, especially my urban colleagues because they often do not have the opportunity to know what is being said about government programs in the farm press.
I thought this article was very important because it was a report from the P.C. policy convention earlier this last August which was billed in the mainstream media as being very much a love-in; that there was very little dissent, that people were happy, they had vision for the future and they were going to ride the great economic boom well into the 21st century, that all kinds of good things were going to happen and all the delegates there were very pleased with everything they saw.
This headline, first of all, caught my eye. It said: "Rural PCs line up at convention to air their gripes". I went on to read:
Conservative farm policies were attacked last week by rural delegates attending the Progressive Conservative national convention.
They said despite official government optimism and selfcongratulations, conditions are bad down on the farm. And government policy is driving rural voters away from Conservatives, they warned.
There was scarcely a word of praise for past government performance or the new theology of market-oriented, subsidy-reduced farm policy being developed and promoted by agriculture minister Don Mazankowski.
As Mazankowski sat in the audience listening, delegate after delegate came to the microphone to complain about the state of the farm economy.
October 3, 1989

They complained about prices, high interest rates, uncertainty caused by government policy and the inequities of the drought program.
Russell Lakusta, of Wandering River in northeastern Alberta, complained that he cannot afford to turn his grain farm over to his son.
"Farmers are in very poor shape", he said. "If we don't get federal help, lower interest rates and get to the point where farmers break even-" At that point, his voice broke and the sentence trailed off.
Later the longtime Conservative said he does not find the government particularly sympathetic to the farmer's plight, despite the record of subsidies.
"I still think the government is sorry for the $3 billion they gave us," he said in an interview. "I don't know why. I think if it hadn't been for Grant Devine's election, we wouldn't have gotten that either."
I might add that another billion dollars would be very welcome in the prairie economy but you can bet the last dollar of those billions that it will not buy Grant Devine another election.
Farmer Bill Cole, from Ninette, Man., was equally blunt.
He was angry about the loss of the interest-free advance payment program this year and the way the drought payment was handled. Payments were late, administration too cumbersome and in too many cases, fanners are being asked to pay back thousands of dollars already received in interim payments, he said in an interview.
On his own farm, Cole received a $7 an acre interim payment and then, instead of the additional payment he expected to cover his bills, he received a notice from Ottawa that he had been overpaid by 52 cents an acre. He has to pay it back.
I might add that the appeal process is in total chaos. The structure that has been set up puts all the burden on rural municipalities which in no way have the resources to deal with what is happening in that drought payment. Reeves and councillors are getting calls in the middle of the night, families are being divided because one brother will get a payment when he had a pretty good crop and the next brother gets nothing, is wiped out and driven out of business. It is causing all kinds of stress in the rural community.
In any event, getting back to the words of Cole, he said:
"That program was a disaster", said Cole, a member of the executive in grains minister Charlie Mayer's constituency organization.
Government Orders
This is one of the Minister of Grains and Oilseeds' own constituency executive members. He said:
"I told Charlie last week to his face, you have two chances for re-election: slim and none."
I think that is pretty blunt talk. I do not think you can put it any clearer than that.
Other delegates had other complaints.
A young Quebec farmer said the government should do more to help young people stay on the land.
An Ontario dairy fanner said reducing government regulation is not the answer.
A Prince Edward Island delegate warned that low prices and a lack of government action will send many family farms into the grasp of multinational, vertically-integrated food companies.
A southern Saskatchewan nurse said farmers are turning to alcohol, drugs and suicide because of poor conditions and a lack of government support.
I might stress again that this is not something dreamed up by wild-eyed New Democrats in some back room. This is a report from the debate at the Conservative convention. These are direct quotes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Who wrote that?

The member opposite asks who wrote that. These are direct quotes from their own delegates and I hope he was there to hear those things said because I think that is very clearly the voice of the whole farm community speaking.
With that I would like to reiterate that the bill we have before us, the bill to charge interest on cash advance payments, is just one more example of this government's agriculture policies that are being rejected from from coast to coast as not only being unworkable but very likely to lead to the demise of agriculture in this country as we know it and to hasten the demise of the most valued institution in rural Canada, the family farm.
This government may think that, as some analysts at their convention said, it does not have to worry about the farm population any more because the Conservative Party has become the party of the upwardly mobile people in the suburbs. If you look at a map of Canada you can see how many constituencies there are that elect rural members in this country. It is not possible for this government to form a government again without rural members. This government may think that farmers cannot remember three years. Farmers can remember a lot longer than that and I hope that the government pays attention to what farmers are saying to them.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like through you to point something out to the previous speaker from Prince Albert. He spoke about the lack of support from this government toward farmers. I want to point out that the minister did say that we had supported government extensively and I want to point out-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The hon. parliamentary secretary may want to participate in the debate at a later stage. Resuming debate, the Hon. Member for Algoma.

Madam Speaker, it is interesting that the parliamentary secretary is so much on the defensive, as was the minister, on this bill. They know they have practically zero support. Even the most militant Tories in this country do not support the bill. It is interesting that some 19 principal farm organizations, commodity groups from across the country, met in Winnipeg yesterday and petitioned the Prime Minister by letter after that meeting demanding that the government withdraw this bill. I did the same thing a week or so ago and lo and behold, the Minister of Agriculture withdrew that bill, C-32. Unfortunately, Bill C-36 is no better than Bill C-32 as regards the interest free cash advances.
It is hard to imagine that the Tbries are really bringing in this legislation. In 1984 they campaigned that they would double the farm cash advance program, and they did, they increased it from $15,000 to $30,000. We supported that move. But lo and behold, when the Budget came down this year they emasculated the benefits of the program because without the interest free portion to the farm cash advance program the program is almost useless. The value will be for somebody who has a crop worth $.5 million who might gain .5 per cent and utilize it because of the mass volume of the program or for someone who is absolutely destitute and cannot get credit any place else.
Farm organizations across this country uniformly are opposed to this program. We would like to spend some time talking about why they are opposed to it. Clearly, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the umbrella group for most Canadian farmers covering the wide spectrum of dairy producers, of fruit and vegetables producers, the pools, the UPA, the Atlantic farm groups,

the Federation of Agriculture from Ontario and the Atlantic Federation of Agriculture all oppose this group. The National Fanners' Union opposes this legislation. As a matter of fact, the group that passed the resolution yesterday and petitioned the Prime Minister said this in a letter to him.
At a national meeting held in Winnipeg this morning, 19 Canadian grain and oilseed producer organizations were unanimous in calling on your government to withdraw Bill C-36, and to re-institute the two previous acts, which provided for interest-free cash advances for crops grown in Canada.
It is interesting that they sum up that letter by saying:
It is urgent to reinstate the 1988/89 Cash Advance Programs, and to allow the farm community with the federal minister, through the policy review process, to design the appropriate marketing systems to ensure competitiveness and equity.
It is signed by the representative, Roy Cusitar, of the United Grain Growers in Winnipeg.
It is supported by all these groups: the Ontario Soybean growers, la federation des producteur de cultures commerciales du Quebec, the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association, the Western Barley Growers, the Alberta Pulse Growers Association, Focus on Inputs, Keystone Agricultural Producers, the Prairie Canola Growers Council, the Manitoba Canola Growers Association, the Saskatchewan Canola Growers Association, the Alberta Soft Wheat Grain Association, the United Grain Growers, the Flax Council of Canada, the Atlantic Grains Council, the Ontario Com Producers Association, the Manitoba Pulse Growers and the Western Canadian Pulse Growers.
There is uniform support to oppose this legislation in every way possible and we just do not understand why the government is proceeding with it. It is just inconceivable to us that the government continues to push to have this legislation. It has been uniformly opposed. The Deputy Prime Minister talked about the enabling legislation that is needed.
All the Government of Canada has to do is obey the law. It is not obeying the law now. The law now says that they will make available to the Canadian Wheat Board and to other commodity groups funds with the interest looked after by the Government of Canada, and they are not doing that. What I am calling on the government to do is to withdraw the bill or just let it die on the Order Paper and to obey the law of Canada now which is to provide interest free cash advances.
Government Orders
The Deputy Prime Minister talked about farmers paying their fair share of the cuts that the government made in government programs. Farmers are making a tremendous contribution. The infamous budget which was brought down will increase taxes and cut services by $5 billion this year and $9 billion next year, and with the goods and services tax a $5.5 billion increase will be imposed the year after. Those are government figures. It may be $9 or $10 billion, but it certainly is going to be the $5.5 billion if the government implement that program.
In this program last spring the government has cut crop insurance by $200 million, grain and flour transportation by $60 million, rail branchline rehabilitation programs by $48 million, and grain and crop advance payment programs by $54 million. That is $27 million a year.
Most of these cuts mean a reduction in services or a reduction in programs to farmers but there is hardly any program, in my opinion, which has the multiplier effect of a grain and crop advance program. I would like to talk about that a little bit later.
Just to respond to the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture saying, "farmers have got to take the blunt axe themselves" let us go on to the other things which they have cut. They have cut the dairy export program by $12 million, the commodity-based loan program by $15 million and the Canadian Dairy Commission by $10 million. So farmers, without being slaughtered on this one, have been slaughtered on a a host of other programs amounting to $400 million, and that does not even get into another $100 million which they are going to have to pay in input costs for the oil and gas excise tax and sales tax. So farmers certainly are taking their chunk of the government's chop.
As we look across the spectrum of Canadian agriculture which is going to be adversely affected by this legislation, we see those organizations which I have mentioned this afternoon such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, and the Canadian Wheat Board Advisory group. This is a farmer elected group across the prairies which advises the Canadian Wheat Board on this. The Canadian Wheat Board operates this program in western Canada. They have opposed it, as have the Saskatchewan Canola Growers Association, the Ontario Com Producers Association, the Manitoba Com Producers Association, and so on.

October 3, 1989
Government Orders
The Deputy Prime Minister this afternoon suggested that the program would have some value, or might continue to operate. That really is not the case because this program, at least in eastern Canada, is operated by farm groups like the Ontario Corn Producers Association. The Ontario Corn Producers Association tells me that at its board meeting just last week it was discussing how many farmers would take advantage of the program that the Deputy Prime Minister is talking about. The program in the past has provided benefits to about 1,200 com producers. Their discussion was as to whether there would be 50 that would even bother taking the benefit, because by the time one pays the administration fee and the other charges, for people who have a very good credit rating there probably is no advantage at all under the program.
So, it is a very big question whether a lot of these associations which have operated the program and done yeoman's service in that regard would even bother. Various organizations have outlined how much harm this program will do. First, the costs are relatively minimal compared to the advantages. It is a relatively inexpensive program compared to many operated by the government, as the Deputy Prime Minister said, costing billions and billions of dollars. So this is a relatively inexpensive program in terms of providing for orderly marketing of Canadian farm commodities, and surely that is the primary goal of the program. It is not just the amount of interest support that is provided, it is the impact on the commodity; the price, the funding and support at a particular moment in time.
Without the program farmers who need the cash will tend to market their commodity as soon as the commodity is harvested. This program allowed them to shift the marketing from the months of October and November into the winter months and the spring months. That had a beneficial effect. It not only kept the price up during the fall months, but it tended to keep the price more stable in the spring months. It not only benefits the
farmer but at the end of the day it benefits the consumer. It does not result in having tremendous troughs when there is a surplus of the commodity in the fall and a shortage in the spring. It tends to level that out.
In the prairies we will see, with this bill destroyed, that farmers will rush to make deliveries in the fall, over-taxing a grain-handling system that does not have as much capacity as it needs to operate without this program.
This program is not trade distorting. It does not increase production. It just provides for a much more orderly marketing arrangement. It does not stimulate production. The government, unilaterally, without the agreement of commodity groups-and certainly the dairy producers-last fall signed an accord at the GATT to not increase government support programs. They did some fast juggling in dairy by cutting out dairy support programs by some $20 million or $25 million and then raised the price of milk by 41 cents a hectolitre, which was less than what they had cut out in the budget.
Nowhere in that GATT accord of last April does this program provide for reducing the support programs. Yet this action by the government results in a reduction.
I guess the other concern we have as we look down through the range of government programs which were destroyed in the budget is that many of these programs which the government chopped out-some $500 million over the next couple of years in support to farmers-are programs that were listed in the free trade deal as being subsidies. The free trade deal also provides for negotiation over the next five to seven years of what is a subsidy, what is an acceptable subsidy that does not encounter countervail or dumping duties. When we look at the budget we see the government, one, two, three, four is removing subsidies while the Americans, who they have not even started to negotiate with in earnest, are not removing any of their subsidies. They are not removing their advance payments or load interest programs. Why are we doing it?

We seem to be doing everything unilaterally, hurting farmers and destroying our negotiating position with the Americans in the trade negotiations which will come up over the next few years.
I spoke earlier about the benefits of this program in terms of not having all your marketing take place at harvest time and spreading it out, having orderly marketing over a period of time. I was interested in what the Ontario Com Producers have indicated as the cost benefits of the program in terms of the price of com. What they have done is they have calculated the price of com during the harvest season, October and November, and then compared it with the selling price of com in the winter, spring and summer months.
It is very interesting to note that the cost benefit in one year, 1987-88 which is the last year for which they have marketing figures in terms of what it cost the government to run the Advance Payments Program and the benefit to the com producers is something like 15 to 1. That is not bad. Even the parliamentary secretary, who is one of the great white bean growers and knows how to calculate how to make profits, would have to admit that a 15 to 1 cost benefit ratio is very good.
If you calculate what the interest on the advance payment program cost the government for the last year for which we have figures, 1987-88, you see it was $1.1 million. The increase in price during the winter, spring and summer months compared to what it was if everybody had marketed in October and November was $16 million, 15 times as much.
Surely even the Tories can calculate that that is good for the industry. It stabilizes it. You do not have massively low prices in October and November, and you do not have massively high prices in the spring because everybody marketed in the fall. If we look at just that one commodity, which is a big important group, although certainly not the whole of the Canadian agriculture scene, you see the tremendous benefits of this.
If you look across the range of commodities, whether you are talking about fruits and vegetables in B.C., Ontario, Quebec, or Atlantic Canada, or if you talk about soybeans, or about the prairie grain, you get a stability in the industry that is very desirable. If you maintain the price as well, it is certainly desirable.
Government Orders
I am suggesting to the government that it really should withdraw, withdraw, withdraw Bill C-36. It is wrong for a country. It is wrong for farm pricing. It is wrong for Canadian farmers, and wrong for agriculture.
I would like to move an amendment to the motion before us today, seconded by the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex:
That Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Advance Payments for Crops
Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act be not now read a
second time but that it be read a second time this day six months
hence.

Madam Speaker, I noticed the statistics show that 3,644 farmers in Ontario took advantage of the advance payments in 1987-88, and a large portion of those were soybean growers, tobacco growers and com producers.
I would like to ask the hon. member what portion of these farmers who took advantage of it in 1987-88 he thinks would still find it a worth-while procedure, a worth-while program under the new bill? That is question number one.
I have a second question which is very close to it. The new bill allows $250,000 instead of the regular level of borrowing that was allowed. I wonder also how many of those 3,644 farmers who took advantage of this would have any reason to use more than the present level of expenditure.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question. He is a person who has taken tremendous interest in agriculture issues. He has worked widely on agriculture issues in the agriculture committee of the House of Commons.
I would suspect that the answer to his inquiry concerning tobacco growers, soybean growers and com growers would be typical of the estimate that has been made by the board of Directors of the Ontario Com Producers Association. They estimate that as low as 50 farmers, out of the 1,200 who have been using the program in the past, might use it in the future. I am not sure of the percentage, but you are getting down to something less than 5 per cent of the people who would use it in the future as it is reconstituted with the farmer paying the interest.
What the government is doing with this bill is destroying the program. They can huff and puff and talk about farmers having to bear the brunt of their cost-cutting exercise and all the rest of it, but if you think that the Ontario Com Producers are going to run a program like

Government Orders
this for 50 producers when in the past they have had something like 1,200 producers, I do not think they will. The administration costs and the overhead and everything grows disproportionately when you are dealing with a very small number of producers compared to a widely diverse group.
The second question is about the $250,000 limit. The current limit is $30,000, $60,000, $90,000 depending on the number of partners in the farming operation. In my opinion, the $250,000 limit is a pure smoke-screen. It is one of two things. As the hon. member will recall, the first bill C-32 was bungled and they were so embarrassed by it that they had to withdraw it because the loan guarantee in the bill did not cover the interest. They had to put up some kind of a smoke-screen to cover the embarrassment of it all and raised the limit to $250,000. In my opinion, that is why they did it.
In any event, very few if any farmers will use it. I think that the amount will never approach the previous limit which was something like 17 per cent in the west and 25 per cent in the east. In any event, it is probably designed to help a few really good Tory supporters who can benefit by the marginal gain they will get on interest. As far as the broad spectrum of the average farmer is concerned, it will benefit practically none, because you are only covering 50 per cent of the grain or the commodity in the bin. I do not know too many farmers who will have half a million dollars worth of grain or other commodity in the bin. In my opinion, it will help practically none.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the member for Algoma if he is indicating to us that he prefers the level to remain at $30,000, $60,000 and $90,000. It would appear from his remarks that he is asking for that level to remain there. Is that what he is indicating?

Madam Speaker, I was responding to the Member for Saskatoon-Humboldt as to the number who I thought would utilize it. In my opinion, there would not be many who would utilize it. What we are asking for-and I want to make this very clear-and what practically every major farm organization in this country is asking for is that the government leave the legislation that is in force now in place, obey the law and provide the money to these farm organizations.
The government should obey the law and give these farm organizations the funds that they are entitled to under the existing Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act and the Crop Advance Payments for Crops Act. That is what I am asking the parliamentary secretary and the government to do. I think if they pay attention to the 19 farm organizations which petitioned the Prime Minister yesterday after the meeting in Winnipeg, that is what they will do.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask my colleague a questioon. I have just received a communication that CIL Agriculture Lambton Works at Cartwright, Ontario, is laying off 150 employees throughout their organization. Will this bill, if it passes in the present form before this House, have a further impact on the farm economy that is reflected here in these lay-offs or are these lay-offs as a direct result of the free trade agreement?

Madam Speaker, I would have to defer to the Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex as I do not know the details of that particular lay-off.
